					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at Infineon Technologies and Technical University of Munich published a technical paper titled “From Physical Devices to RTL Models: Abstraction and Validation in Hardware Engineering.” Abstract: “This paper introduces the foundational principles underlying hardware engineering models and argues that abstraction is their defining characteristic. Because abstraction necessarily omits detail and constrains what engineers can... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/tracing-hardware-design-from-physical-devices-to-rtl-infineon-tu-munich/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/tracing-hardware-design-from-physical-devices-to-rtl-infineon-tu-munich/">Tracing Hardware Design From Physical Devices to RTL (Infineon, TU Munich)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at Infineon Technologies and Technical University of Munich published a technical paper titled “From Physical Devices to RTL Models: Abstraction and Validation in Hardware Engineering.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract:</strong></p>
<p>“This paper introduces the foundational principles underlying hardware engineering models and argues that abstraction is their defining characteristic. Because abstraction necessarily omits detail and constrains what engineers can build, models are inherently incomplete in specific respects &#8211; or, as George Box famously observed, &#8220;All models are wrong, but some are useful&#8221;. At the same time, abstraction is essential for simplification, which is key to managing complexity. More abstract models also tend to simulate faster because fewer details must be considered.</p>
<p>This paper subsequently examines a range of abstraction methods in digital design &#8211; sometimes referred to as design disciplines &#8211; including lumped models, value-discrete models, and time-discrete models. Together with constraints that define the validity of the abstraction and design guidelines, these abstraction methods establish design disciplines. This paper further relates these forms of abstraction to pre-clustered design elements such as transistors, gates, registers, and transfer functions. These pre-clustered elements define abstraction levels, such as the gate level, and are presented as a key enabler of increased design productivity.”</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01186">Find the technical paper here</a>. October 2026.</p>
<p>Ecker, Wolfgang, Natalie Simson, Johannes Ecker, and Endri Kaja. “From Physical Devices to RTL Models: Abstraction and Validation in Hardware Engineering.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.01186 (October 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.01186</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/tracing-hardware-design-from-physical-devices-to-rtl-infineon-tu-munich/">Tracing Hardware Design From Physical Devices to RTL (Infineon, TU Munich)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/hbf-for-high-throughput-llm-serving-uc-berkeley-furiosaai/">HBF for High-Throughput LLM Serving (UC Berkeley, FuriosaAI)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Researchers at the <strong>UC Berkeley</strong> and <strong>FuriosaAI</strong> published a technical paper titled “Characterizing High Bandwidth Flash for LLM Serving.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Abstract</strong></p>
<p>“Large language model (LLM) serving requires substantial memory to store model weights and KV caches. As models grow larger and contexts become longer, memory capacity and bandwidth increasingly become bottlenecks for serving performance. Agentic workloads compound this pressure through repeated interactions over growing contexts, making it increasingly important to retain KV state for reuse. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) offers a way to expand accelerator memory capacity for large language model (LLM) serving, but its access costs and limited write endurance complicate its use. We evaluate HBF for high-throughput agentic serving across system design and scheduling choices to understand when additional capacity improves serving performance and energy efficiency. We introduce an HBM-HBF-host hierarchical storage system and buffered cache-aware scheduling, and use trace-driven simulations to analyze their effects on performance, energy consumption, and HBF write lifetime. Across the evaluated workloads, the fastest HBF-augmented systems reduce completion time by 36.1-87.0% relative to HBM-only systems. Modeled energy savings reach 55.8%, although HBF increases energy consumption on some light workloads. Buffered cache-aware scheduling extends estimated HBF write lifetime from 4.77 to 14.82 years in the evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate the importance of coordinating data placement and scheduling to improve serving efficiency while sustaining a practical HBF write lifetime.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39131">Find the technical paper here</a>. September 2026.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Yu, Zack, Chloe Wong, Coleman Hooper, Minjae Lee, Wonjun Kang, Youngjin Cho, Michael W. Mahoney, Yakun Sophia Shao, Kurt Keutzer, and Amir Gholami. “Characterizing High Bandwidth Flash for LLM Serving.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.39131 (September 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.39131</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">&nbsp;</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/hbf-for-high-throughput-llm-serving-uc-berkeley-furiosaai/">HBF for High-Throughput LLM Serving (UC Berkeley, FuriosaAI)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at Georgia Institute of Technology, Qatar Computing Research Institute, and Purdue University published a technical paper titled “A Formal Security Analysis of CAN XL.” Abstract: &#8220;For decades, the Controller Area Network (CAN) has been the backbone of in-vehicle communication. As modern vehicles integrate cameras, LiDARs, and AI components, classic CAN (CAN CC) faces growing... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/formal-analysis-uncovers-security-flaws-in-can-xl-georgia-tech-qcri-purdue/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/formal-analysis-uncovers-security-flaws-in-can-xl-georgia-tech-qcri-purdue/">Formal Automotive Security Analysis Of CAN XL  (Georgia Tech, QCRI, Purdue)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at Georgia Institute of Technology, Qatar Computing Research Institute, and Purdue University published a technical paper titled “A Formal Security Analysis of CAN XL.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract:</strong></p>
<p>&#8220;For decades, the Controller Area Network (CAN) has been the backbone of in-vehicle communication. As modern vehicles integrate cameras, LiDARs, and AI components, classic CAN (CAN CC) faces growing limitations in bandwidth, functionality, and security. To fill these gaps, CAN XL was introduced as the next generation of CAN, aiming to offer longer payloads, higher bandwidth, and enhanced security.</p>
<p>CAN XL makes significant standard-level changes across multiple stack layers. It also introduces several security features, but it is unclear whether these are mere add-on extensions or whether the standard redesign itself tackles CAN&#8217;s chronic security weakness: the MAC sub-layer. This sub-layer governs frame formats and error handling and has historically enabled many CAN CC attacks. As the industry transitions to CAN XL, the security posture of its yet-unexplored MAC sub-layer must be understood before widespread deployment.</p>
<p>This paper presents the first security analysis of the CAN XL standard, focusing on its MAC sub-layer. We develop a bit-precise CAN XL formal model and release it to facilitate future research. We design a formal analysis workflow guided by CAN XL&#8217;s field-oriented structure to uncover vulnerabilities. Contrary to expectations, our analysis shows that CAN XL remains vulnerable to all known CAN CC MAC sub-layer issues while introducing seven new vulnerabilities, arguably worsening security. We validate them using commercial CAN XL controllers and demonstrate exploitability via two multi-stage attacks on a testbed simulating real vehicle traffic. Finally, we propose mitigations including formally verifying standard revisions that could prevent several attacks.&#8221;</p>
<p><a href="https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/tang-zhaozhou">Find the technical paper here</a>. August 2026.</p>
<p>Tang, Zhaozhou, Khaled Serag, Z. Berkay Celik, Vijay Ganesh, Saman Zonouz, and Raheem Beyah. “A Formal Security Analysis of CAN XL.” In 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 26), 2227–2246. Baltimore, MD: USENIX Association, August 2026. https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity26/presentation/tang-zhaozhou</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/formal-analysis-uncovers-security-flaws-in-can-xl-georgia-tech-qcri-purdue/">Formal Automotive Security Analysis Of CAN XL  (Georgia Tech, QCRI, Purdue)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<item>
		<title>The Proof Economy</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/the-proof-economy/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/the-proof-economy/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Vidya Chandran Darbari]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Fri, 02 Oct 2026 07:01:52 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - SLD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Making Formal Normal]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[System-Level Design]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Axiomise]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[formal]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[formal verification]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[proofs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[verification]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282276</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>As artificial intelligence makes creation abundant, proof becomes the new scarcity.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-proof-economy/">The Proof Economy</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Across my career, from medicine and life sciences into structural biology, higher education and later semiconductor verification, I have kept meeting the same fundamental challenge in different forms.</p>
<p><strong>How do we know something is true?</strong></p>
<p>Scientists speak of reproducibility. Physicians of evidence. Educators of understanding. Engineers of verification. Beneath the terminology lies a common objective: <i>establishing confidence before action.</i></p>
<h2>Why this question matters now</h2>
<p>As a founder, I use AI daily. It drafts, summarises, explains, and occasionally surprises me with the elegance of what it produces. It has changed the pace at which I think and act as an executive.</p>
<p>Yet the more I use it, the more I notice a quiet friction: <i>The output looks finished. It reads confidently. But before every decision that matters, I still have to ask: do I trust this enough to act on it?</i></p>
<p>That question, once asked mainly in the laboratory or the verification lab, is now asked in the boardroom, the classroom and the consulting room. The urgency is not that AI has become dangerous, but that it has become good enough to be believed without being verified.</p>
<p>What follows is not a survey. It is my own reading of a shift I have watched from four vantage points: the wet lab, the university, the boardroom and the verification lab. The disciplines look nothing alike from the outside. From the inside, they have been converging on the same question for some time. AI has only made it louder.</p>
<h2>Science: Prediction is not discovery</h2>
<p>The tension between prediction and proof is perhaps most visible in science.</p>
<p>Proteins form the molecular machines that run every cell, and their three-dimensional shape determines what they do: how a pathogen injects DNA into a host, how an antibiotic binds its target, how an enzyme catalyses a reaction. For half a century, discovering that shape was led by laborious experimental work. AlphaFold, released by DeepMind in 2020, changed that. Given only a protein sequence, it predicts the folded structure in minutes, at accuracies that in many cases rival experiment. The leap is real. It is also easy to misread.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282277" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig1.webp?resize=1379%2C693&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1379" height="693" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig1.webp?w=1379&amp;ssl=1 1379w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C151&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C515&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C386&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C302&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p>My own training was as an experimental structural biologist, first using X-ray crystallography and later single-particle cryo-electron microscopy to solve the architectures of large bacterial machines: the type IV secretion system that Gram-negative pathogens use to inject DNA and toxins, and the RNA polymerase complexes that read genes into RNA. Neither project started with the structure. They started with a biological question: <i>how does this machine open, gate, translocate, switch state?</i></p>
<p>The structure was a means to that question, not an end in itself.</p>
<p>Everything downstream depended on how honestly the atomic model reflected the experimental evidence, the diffraction data in a crystallographic map or the density in a cryo-EM reconstruction. A side chain placed one rotamer too confidently, a loop built where the density did not support it, and the mechanistic story built on top would quietly drift away from reality. The discipline was as much about restraint as ambition: build only what the data can carry.</p>
<p>AlphaFold accelerated the early stages of that work dramatically. Starting models that once took months of molecular replacement or manual building could be generated in hours. Yet the underlying discipline did not change.</p>
<p>An independent assessment in <i>Nature Methods</i> concluded that AlphaFold&#8217;s predictions are best treated as &#8220;exceptionally useful hypotheses&#8221;, highly accurate on average, yet with roughly 10% of the most confident predictions still deviating from experimental structures by more than 2 Å (<a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-023-02087-4">Terwilliger et al., 2024</a>).</p>
<p>A prediction, however elegant, still had to be reconciled with the data.</p>
<p>That principle that a model must correspond to evidence rather than merely appear plausible is the same one that governs verification in engineering. The language differs. The discipline does not.</p>
<h2>Medicine: Confidence is a clinical requirement</h2>
<p>I came to structural biology through medicine. Twenty-five years ago, I sat on the other side of this question, as a medical student at King Edward Memorial Hospital in Mumbai, learning how a diagnosis is defended. The tools were textbooks, cadavers, bedside teaching and long viva examinations in front of consultants who did not settle for the right answer if you could not defend the reasoning behind it.</p>
<p>Diagnostic confidence was not an intuition. It was a chain of evidence: a differential considered and ruled out, a treatment justified against alternatives.</p>
<p>That discipline scaled poorly, bounded by the memory of individual clinicians and the time they had for each patient. AI is now genuinely helping where it was hardest to sustain, matching or exceeding specialists on narrow, well-scoped tasks as I hear from my friends. Where it has landed responsibly, it has extended access rather than replaced judgement.</p>
<p>Yet, clinical adoption still depends on prospective validation and accountability, not algorithmic performance alone. As a person on the other side of the table now rather than a clinician, I notice the shift in myself. I welcome the speed of an AI-assisted read. I still want to know a human took responsibility for the decision that acts on it.</p>
<p>Patients do not seek the most probable answer, but the most reliable.</p>
<h2>Education: An improvement challenge, not a detection problem</h2>
<p>For generations, producing an answer was accepted as evidence of learning. Generative AI has made that assumption fragile. Essays, code and sophisticated analyses can now be produced in seconds. Chasing this with ever-better detectors misreads the problem. Detection is a policing frame. What has actually changed is the assessment target: understanding can no longer be inferred from a finished artefact alone. Education has been handed an improvement challenge, not a plagiarism one.</p>
<p>I spent more than nine years as an educator at Queen Mary University of London, teaching biochemistry and structural biology to undergraduates and postgraduates, and became a Fellow of the Higher Education Academy along the way. Long before generative AI, the honest question in a classroom was always the same one: has this student understood, or have they reproduced? A well-written essay could hide either. So could a correctly worked problem. The teachers I learned most from asked follow-up questions. They watched students draw a mechanism on the board. They ran lab reports as conversations, not as marking exercises.</p>
<p>Assessment, done well, has always been a dialogue.</p>
<p>What generative AI has done is remove the last comfortable hiding places for that lazier version of assessment, the one that graded the artefact and inferred the mind behind it.</p>
<p>Universities that respond by tightening detection are trying to preserve a shortcut. Universities that respond by rebuilding around dialogue, oral examinations, staged submissions, in-class problem solving and process-graded work, are finally being pushed to do what good teachers already knew they should. The tools have caught up with the standard, not undermined it.</p>
<p>The classroom I remember at Queen Mary and the training rooms that Axiomise now runs for practicing engineers are asking the same question in different vocabulary. Can the learner walk through the reasoning, defend the choice, explain why one approach holds and another does not, and reproduce the argument on something they have not seen before? AI can accelerate every part of that preparation. It cannot answer for the learner.</p>
<p>The challenge is no longer proof of completion. It is proof of comprehension.</p>
<h2>Semiconductors and autonomous systems: The cost of uncertainty</h2>
<p>Testing can show that a system works under specific conditions; it cannot show that failures are absent under all conditions. The semiconductor industry learned this the hard way. As designs grew to billions of transistors and moved into safety-critical systems from pacemakers to avionics, simulation alone could not deliver assurance. Formal verification emerged as the mathematical discipline that reasons about all possible behaviours of a design, not only those a testbench happens to exercise.</p>
<p>Autonomous vehicles are confronting the same lesson publicly. In July 2026, the U.S. NHTSA issued a call to action after documenting cases of autonomous vehicles driving into active emergency scenes, noting that &#8220;emergency scenes are not rare or extreme edge cases&#8221; (<a href="https://www.thestreet.com/technology/nhtsa-warns-tesla-waymo-serious-issue">TheStreet, 2026</a>). Regulators are moving in step: the EU AI Act&#8217;s conformity assessment regime for high-risk AI systems begins applying in August 2026 (<a href="https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43/">EU AI Act Article 43</a>).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282278" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig2.webp?resize=451%2C254&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="451" height="254" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig2.webp?w=451&amp;ssl=1 451w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Axiomise_The-Proof-Economy-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w" sizes="(max-width: 451px) 100vw, 451px" /></p>
<p>The chip inside the car and the software driving it face the question formal verification has answered for decades: can we show absence of failure, not merely absence of observed failure?</p>
<h2>The emergence of the proof economy</h2>
<p>Every technological revolution creates a new bottleneck. The Industrial Revolution reduced the scarcity of physical production; the Information Revolution, the scarcity of information; the AI Revolution is reducing the scarcity of creation itself. As creation becomes abundant, validation becomes scarce.</p>
<p>Whether validating a protein structure, a medical diagnosis, a student&#8217;s understanding or the behaviour of an autonomous system, the question is the same:</p>
<p><strong>Not whether something appears to work, but whether we can demonstrate why it should be trusted.</strong></p>
<h2>A reflection from a conference floor</h2>
<p>This year I attended various conferences from Silicon Valley to India, and I walked the floor, spoke to many, and heard the chatter in the halls. In the exhibition hall around us, half the conversations were about what AI can now generate. On the panel in front of me, the conversation was almost entirely about what it should have to prove before it is trusted in a car, a train, in healthcare, the sensors around us. Different rooms, different disciplines, the same underlying question.</p>
<p>Walking out of the venues afterwards, I thought about how far the road to Axiomise for me had run. From the corridors of King Edward Memorial Hospital in Mumbai, to a Cambridge crystallography lab, to a Queen Mary lecture theatre, to the audience of industry events where the question on the table was the one that had followed me from the wards. How do we know?</p>
<p>The age of productivity is already here.</p>
<p>The question is whether we can build the discipline, the training and the institutions to make the age of proof match it.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-proof-economy/">The Proof Economy</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Autonomous workflow design; CFETs push scaling beyond 10 angstroms; onsemi-Synaptics deal revised; physical AI M&#038;A and funding; AI data centers drive new power/packaging investments; new Spectre-v2 attack targets JIT compilers; photonics moves closer to compute; quantum HW; false base station risks; 88k engineers needed.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-158/">Chip Industry Week In Review</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<h3><strong>Top of the Week</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Synopsys</strong> unveiled a portfolio of domain-specific <a href="https://news.synopsys.com/2026-09-28-Synopsys-Powers-Autonomous-Engineering-with-a-Broad-Portfolio-of-Long-Horizon-Agents-and-Autopilot-Platform?utm_source=chatgpt.com">long-horizon agents</a> that can reason, plan, and execute multi-step engineering workflows across verification, system validation, implementation, analog, manufacturing, simulation and analysis. Synopsys also inked a multi-year agreement with <strong>OpenAI</strong> to develop GPT-Synopsys, a <a href="https://news.synopsys.com/2026-09-30-OpenAI-and-Synopsys-Announce-GPT-Synopsys-Frontier-Intelligence-to-Revolutionize-Chip-Design">specialized model</a> optimized to use its EDA tools for semiconductor design workflows.</li>
<li><strong>Semiconductor Engineering</strong> released its <a href="https://semiengineering.com/photonics-fundamentals-for-electronics-engineers-ebook/">Photonics eBook</a>, an in-depth look at the technologies, applications, and ongoing research that will be needed to address the growing bandwidth problem in data centers and semiconductor packages.</li>
<li><strong><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignright" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-01-at-9.51.49-AM.png?resize=164%2C157&#038;ssl=1" width="164" height="157" />Lam Research</strong> proposed a <a href="https://newsroom.lamresearch.com/self-aligned-cfet-architecture-cmos-scaling">self-aligned CFET architecture</a> (right) that could extend CMOS scaling below 10 angstroms. Its digital-twin modeling produced a 0.0094 μm² 6T SRAM bit cell, which is 52.7% smaller than N3 technology, while maintaining at least a 10 nm overlay window across critical contact layers.</li>
<li><strong>TSMC</strong> is reportedly evaluating a semiconductor <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-01/tsmc-mulls-multibillion-dollar-texas-campus-for-more-ai-chips">manufacturing investment in Texas </a>that would expand its U.S. production footprint beyond its $265B Arizona buildout, per Bloomberg.</li>
<li><strong>S. Korea</strong>’s <a href="https://www.motir.go.kr/kor/article/ATCL3f49a5a8c/172254/view">semiconductor exports surged</a> over 262% year over year to a record $60B in September, driven by stronger memory demand, higher shipment volumes and rising memory prices.</li>
</ul>
<h2 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><a href="http://hms.ceratizit.com/jatnEn"><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24281643" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/onlinebanner_HMS-Semiconductor_1270x240px_V1.jpg?resize=968%2C184&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="968" height="184" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/onlinebanner_HMS-Semiconductor_1270x240px_V1.jpg?resize=300%2C57&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/onlinebanner_HMS-Semiconductor_1270x240px_V1.jpg?resize=1024%2C194&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/onlinebanner_HMS-Semiconductor_1270x240px_V1.jpg?resize=768%2C145&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/onlinebanner_HMS-Semiconductor_1270x240px_V1.jpg?resize=600%2C113&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/onlinebanner_HMS-Semiconductor_1270x240px_V1.jpg?w=1270&amp;ssl=1 1270w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 968px) 100vw, 968px" /></a></h2>
<h3><strong>Threats and defenses</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>VUSec</strong> and <strong>SSSA</strong> researchers uncovered Branch Target Reuse, a new <a href="https://www.vusec.net/projects/btr/">Spectre-v2 attack</a> targeting just-in-time compilers. They demonstrated an end-to-end Linux attack that can leak arbitrary memory — including a root password hash — even with existing Spectre defenses enabled. Hardware vendors said existing mitigation mechanisms can address BTR, with protections deployed through software.</li>
<li><strong>Nvidia</strong> launched its <a href="https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-Launches-Open-Agent-Safety-Platform-to-Secure-Agents-From-Testing-to-Deployment/default.aspx">Open Agent Safety Platform</a>, combining open-source software with hardware-based controls for agentic AI security. Its Sentry reference design runs on BlueField-4 DPUs to monitor agent behavior and enforce security policies independently in silicon, quarantining agents that move outside defined boundaries. <strong>Cadence</strong> is <a href="https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/corporate-news/posts/trusted-autonomy-with-cadence-ai-super-agents-and-nvidia-agent-safety-platform">integrating the platform</a> with its AI Super Agents to add runtime controls around autonomous chip-design workflows.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Physical AI</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>AMD</strong> plans to <a href="https://newsroom.amd.com/news/amd-acquire-world-labs/">acquire</a> <strong>World Labs</strong>, which develops spatial-intelligence AI models that simulate interactive 3D environments for robotics. The $8.2B all-stock deal is expected to close by the end of 2026.</li>
<li><strong>SiMa.ai</strong> raised $150M to develop <a href="https://sima.ai/press-release/sima-ai-reaches-1-45b-valuation-with-500-million-in-total-funding-to-scale-physical-ai-in-humanoids-automotive-and-drones/">physical AI</a> solutions, including silicon with 1,000+ TOPS and an agentic software environment.</li>
<li>Physical AI is pushing more intelligence into edge devices, where systems must <a href="https://semiengineering.com/turning-edge-ai-data-into-real-time-action/">turn sensor data into real-time action</a>, increasing demands for compute, memory, connectivity, power efficiency, and security.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Capacity</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong> Infineon</strong> opened the first phase of a new <a href="https://www.infineon.com/press-release/2026/infpr202610-144">backend manufacturing hub in Bangkok</a>, adding semiconductor assembly, test and wafer-test capacity.</li>
<li><strong>Samsung Electro-Mechanics</strong> will invest about US $4.9B to expand <a href="https://m.samsungsem.com/jp/newsroom/news/view.do?id=10563">FCBGA package-substrate capacity</a> in South Korea and Vietnam for AI servers. Also, <strong>TOPPAN</strong> opened its <a href="https://www.holdings.toppan.com/en/news/2026/09/newsrelease260930_1.html">first overseas FC-BGA substrate</a> production site in Singapore, targeting large, high-layer-count substrates for AI processors and networking equipment.</li>
<li><strong>VSMC</strong>, the <strong>VIS-NXP</strong> joint venture, <a href="https://investors.nxp.com/news-releases/news-release-details/vsmc-celebrates-grand-opening-its-first-300mm-fab-singapore">opened its 300mm fab</a> in Singapore and is also reportedly considering a <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-28/tsmc-affiliate-plans-second-singapore-chip-plant-in-asia-push">second Singapore fab</a>.</li>
</ul>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24282247" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/261001-Infineon-BKK-Opening-29.jpg?resize=596%2C397&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="596" height="397" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/261001-Infineon-BKK-Opening-29-scaled.jpg?resize=300%2C200&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/261001-Infineon-BKK-Opening-29-scaled.jpg?resize=1024%2C683&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/261001-Infineon-BKK-Opening-29-scaled.jpg?resize=768%2C512&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/261001-Infineon-BKK-Opening-29-scaled.jpg?resize=1536%2C1024&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/261001-Infineon-BKK-Opening-29-scaled.jpg?resize=2048%2C1365&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/261001-Infineon-BKK-Opening-29-scaled.jpg?resize=600%2C400&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 596px) 100vw, 596px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Infineon&#8217;s new backend manufacturing hub in Bangkok, Thailand</strong></p>
<h3><strong>Memory</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Micron</strong> says memory supply will remain <a href="https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/mu/transcripts/699706-q4-2026/?">tight through 2028</a>, with more than 75% of its 2027 output already committed. It also said 2027 HBM pricing will be significantly higher than 2026 levels. Micron reported record Q4 <a href="https://micron.gcs-web.com/node/50991">revenue of $54B,</a> up from $11B a year earlier.</li>
<li>HBM is expected to consume nearly <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/samsung-electronics-says-hbm-account-nearly-30-industry-dram-capacity-next-year-2026-09-29/">30% of DRAM manufacturers’ wafer capacity</a> in 2027, up from about 20% currently, a <strong>Samsung</strong> executive told Reuters.</li>
<li><strong>Teradyne</strong> introduced its Magnum E2 <a href="https://investors.teradyne.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/451/teradyne-announces-magnum-e2-to-address-next-generation-memory-test-demands-driven-by-ai-and-high-performance-computing">high-speed memory test system</a>, supporting next-generation LPDDR6 and DDR6, as well as GDDR7 and NAND flash for growing AI and HPC memory requirements.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Photonics</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><b>JEDEC</b> published the industry’s first <span draggable="true"><a href="https://www.jedec.org/news/pressreleases/jedec%C2%AE-publishes-first-industry-wide-silicon-photonics-reliability-standard-ai" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">silicon photonics reliability standard</a></span>, establishing common qualification and reliability requirements as optical interconnects scale for AI and data-center systems.</li>
<li><strong>Counterpoint</strong> says <a href="https://counterpointresearch.com/en/insights/five-infrastructure-trends-to-watch-from-the-ai-infra-summit">network bottlenecks are becoming a bigger constraint</a> on AI accelerator performance, with GPUs spending roughly 12.5% of their time waiting on the network in some workloads. The firm expects near-packaged optics to begin sampling in late 2026 or early 2027, followed by CPO as AI systems demand faster, more power-efficient scale-up interconnects.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Global"><strong>Global</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Americas</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>California</strong> now exempts certain chemical mixtures containing 70% or less gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) from state permitting, reporting, and other regulatory requirements. GBL is used as a <a href="https://sd15.senate.ca.gov/news/california-will-continue-be-leader-semiconductor-manufacturing-senator-corteses-sb-1306-signed">solvent in semiconductor photoresists</a>. Controls on pure GBL remain.</li>
<li><strong>Lam Research</strong> opened a 470k-sq.ft. <a href="https://newsroom.lamresearch.com/silicon-valley-semiconductor-warehouse-built-for-velocity-resilience">logistics and supply hub</a> in Livermore, California.</li>
<li><strong>S. Korea</strong> and the <strong>U.S.</strong> are advancing a $22B gas-fired power project in <strong>Texas</strong>, part of a broader Korea-U.S. strategic investment package of up to $350B. The 6.47-GW project is aimed at meeting rising <a href="https://www.motir.go.kr/kor/article/ATCL3f49a5a8c/172253/view?mno=&amp;pageIndex=1">power demand</a> from semiconductor plants and AI data centers.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Europe</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Fraunhofer IAF</strong> announced newly launched research initiatives in <a href="https://www.iaf.fraunhofer.de/en/media-library/press-releases/Fraunhofer-IAF-at-EFX2026.html">AI-assisted chip design and chips for AI applications</a>, including AI-accelerated CMOS design and hardware for edge AI. The institute is also showcasing its III-V semiconductor pilot-line capabilities for heterogeneous integration and chip manufacturing.</li>
<li><strong>Global Electronics Association</strong> and the <strong>Fraunhofer Group for Microelectronics</strong> signed an agreement to accelerate <a href="https://www.electronics.org/news-release/global-electronics-association-and-fraunhofer-group-microelectronics-sign-mou-support">industrial adoption of advanced packaging</a> technologies.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Asia</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Semifive</strong> inked a deal with <strong>Mobilint</strong> to develop a <a href="https://semifive.com/company/newsroom/press-releases/">robotics AI processor</a> under <strong>South Korea</strong>’s K-On-Device AI Semiconductor program.</li>
<li><strong>Air Liquide</strong> will invest more than US$193M in production units supplying ultra-pure gases to support the expansion of an existing advanced logic-chip <a href="https://www.airliquide.com/group/press-releases-news/2026-09-30/air-liquide-invests-over-170-million-euros-support-semiconductor-leader-expanding-manufacturing">fab in southern Japan</a>.</li>

<h2 id="Reports and Deals"><strong>Reports and Deals</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>More deals</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Infineon</strong> will supply SiC power devices for <strong>Eaton</strong>’s MVSST 2.0 solid-state transformer platform, designed to support emerging <a href="https://www.infineon.com/press-release/2026/infpr202609-146?">800 VDC architectures for high-density AI data centers.</a></li>
<li><strong>onsemi</strong> <a href="https://investor.synaptics.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-and-synaptics-announce-revised-merger-agreement">revised its planned acquisition</a> of <strong>Synaptics</strong> to a $5.7B all-cash deal, offering $123 per share, after Synaptics received an unsolicited competing proposal. The original June agreement was valued at approximately $7B.</li>
<li><strong>Amazon</strong> broadened its use of <strong>Synopsys</strong> products to include application-optimized <a href="https://news.synopsys.com/2026-09-30-Synopsys-and-Amazon-Announce-Strategic,-Multi-year-IP-Agreement-for-Custom-Silicon-Collaboration-Also-Extends-to-Cloud-and-AI-Powered-Engineering">silicon IP</a> for custom chips and AWS infrastructure, with the companies also planning custom agentic-AI capabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Anthropic’</strong>s IPO filing revealed that it is the customer behind <strong>Broadcom</strong>’s previously disclosed <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/broadcom-lend-anthropic-up-42-billion-lease-its-chips-filing-says-2026-10-01/">AI compute-financing arrangement of up to $42B.</a></li>
<li><strong>Applied Materials</strong> added <strong>Kioxia</strong> and <strong>Besi</strong> as partners at its $5B EPIC Center, expanding work on <a href="https://www.appliedmaterials.com/us/en/newsroom/press-releases/09292026-kioxia-partner-at-epic-center.html">next-gen memory</a> and <a href="https://ir.appliedmaterials.com/node/29676/pdf">advanced packaging</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Samsung</strong> will invest a combined <a href="https://news.samsung.com/in/samsung-to-invest-usd-1-billion-in-ai-infrastructure-company-helix">$1B in Helix Digital Infrastructure</a>, an integrated AI infrastructure spanning hyperscale data centers, power generation and transmission, and fiber-optic networks.</li>
<li><strong>Tanaka</strong> began a collaboration with <strong>TNO/CITC</strong> to develop and evaluate next-generation <a href="https://tanaka-preciousmetals.com/en/news/information/20261001.html">semiconductor-packaging materials</a>, including silver- and copper-based adhesive pastes for die and clip bonding.</li>
<li><strong>DeepSeek</strong> will develop <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/deepseek-partners-with-huawei-develop-chip-programming-tools-reducing-reliance-2026-09-30/">programming tools</a> optimized for <strong>Huawei</strong>&#8216;s AI chips, including compute and communication libraries, per Reuters.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Fundings, IPO</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>CScale</strong> exited stealth with $145M in funding to commercialize an <a href="https://www.cscale.ai/press/cscale-exits-stealth">optical interconnect</a> for AI scale-up that is architected to contain optical failures without interrupting compute.</li>
<li><strong>Efficient Computer</strong> raised $97M to ship its energy-efficient <a href="https://www.efficient.computer/resources/announces-97m-raise-to-scale-its-processors-from-physical-ai-to-the-datacenter">general-purpose processor</a> in volume and scale the architecture to data center-class performance.</li>
<li><strong>Volantis</strong> raised $88M for its <a href="https://volantissemi.ai/news-insights/our-88m-series-a-demolishing-the-memory-wall-with-photonics-post">optical interconnect</a> that uses integrated micro-VCSELs to connect large numbers of memory chips into a unified pool for AI inference.</li>
<li><strong>Zenithon AI</strong> raised $10M to develop <a href="https://seraphim.vc/news/zenithon-raises-10m-ai-world-models-engineering-physics/">AI world models</a> for extreme physics applications, including semiconductor manufacturing.</li>
<li><strong>SK hynix</strong>&#8216;s U.S. subsidiary <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/sk-hynixs-solidigm-weighs-ipo-that-could-value-the-unit-up-150-billion-sources-2026-09-25/">Solidigm is pondering an IPO</a>, reports Reuters. SK says <a href="https://news.skhynix.com/en/fact-11/">nothing</a> has been decided.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Reports</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Revenue across the broader semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem, including foundries, IDMs, packaging and test, reached a record $96.6B in 2Q26, <a href="https://counterpointresearch.com/en/insights/global-foundry-20-revenue-rises-25-yoy-to-a-record-966-billion-in-as-advanced">up 25% YoY</a>, reports <strong>Counterpoint.</strong></li>
<li>Conventional DRAM contract prices are expected to rise <a href="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260930-13258.html">10% to 15% in 4Q26</a> and NAND flash prices 15% to 20%, per TrendForce. Enterprise SSD bit demand is projected to grow more than 80% in 2026.</li>
<li><strong>Bain </strong>says AI has reversed the long-running advantage of software over hardware, with <a href="https://www.bain.com/insights/hardware-strikes-back-in-the-ai-era-technology-report-2026/?utm_source=chatgpt.com">semiconductor and hardware stocks growing at a 24% compound annual rate</a> from 2020 to 2026 versus 6% for software.</li>
<li>N. American <a href="https://www.electronics.org/news-release/north-american-ems-orders-outpace-shipments-august-bookings-rise-535-year-over-year">EMS</a> and <a href="https://www.electronics.org/news-release/north-american-pcb-shipments-jump-235-august-extending-strong-2026-growth">PCB shipments</a> for August 2026 (<strong>Global Electronics</strong>)</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="New Technologies"><strong>New Technologies</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Test, measurement, and failure analysis</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Keysight</strong> introduced a 20 GHz dual-channel <a href="https://www.keysight.com/us/en/about/newsroom/catalog/news-release.2026.0929_pr26-096-keysight-introduces-dual-channel-analog-signal-generatoror-advanced-device-testing.html">analog signal generator</a> with ultra-low noise, calibrated output power, and software mode switching to optimize performance across different applications.</li>
<li><strong>Hamamatsu Photonics</strong> developed an inverted emission microscope for <a href="https://www.hamamatsu.com/us/en/news/products-and-technologies/2026/20260929000000.html">failure analysis of advanced packages</a> including HBM, AI chiplets, and 2.5D/3D devices.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Compute, embedded, and engineering tools</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>AMD</strong> started sampling a Versal adaptive SoC in a space-grade <a href="https://newsroom.amd.com/news/amd-sampling-versal-ai-core-adaptive-soc/">organic lidless package</a> designed to support missions lasting up to 15 years. AMD also introduced an agentic AI assistant to accelerate the <a href="https://newsroom.amd.com/news/amd-ross-agentic-ai-embedded-design-development/">embedded development</a> flow.</li>
<li><strong>Siemens</strong> announced several updates to <span draggable="true"><a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-simcenter-testlab-summer-2026/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">its Simcenter Testlab engineering software</a></span>, including improvements to how the system aids structural dynamics, system NVH prediction, and AI-ready data preparation workflows.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Connectivity and memory</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Infineon</strong> expanded its USB 20Gbps ecosystem with a <a href="https://www.infineon.com/technology-news/2026/inftn202609-148">PCIe Gen4 x4 add-on card</a>, a 10-meter <a href="https://www.infineon.com/technology-news/2026/inftn202609-147">USB 3.2 Gen 2&#215;2 active optical cable</a> developed with EverProX, and a <a href="https://www.infineon.com/technology-news/2026/inftn202609-149">20Gbps USB connectivity collaboration</a> with ASMedia.</li>
<li><strong>Everspin</strong> demonstrated what it says is the <a href="https://investor.everspin.com/news-releases/news-release-details/everspin-demonstrates-worlds-first-cxl-connected-mram-snia">first CXL-connected MRAM platform</a>, creating a persistent-memory tier between DRAM and NAND.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Adoptions &amp; wins</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Siemens</strong> said naval engineering company Caponnetto Hueber used its <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-caponnetto-hueber-simcenter-bgf45/">digital-twin technology</a> to improve hydrodynamic performance and sustainability in vessel design.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2 id="Research"><strong>Research</strong></h2>
<p><strong>University of Tokyo, NTU</strong> and others grew boron carbon nitride as a <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11047-9">high-performance p-type</a> semiconductor, with hole mobility up to 100 cm²/V·s, on-current above 0.9 mA/μm, and on/off ratios up to 10⁸.</p>
<p><strong>Purdue</strong> and <strong>UCLA</strong> &#8220;experimentally quantify the impact of <a href="https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/aelm.70600">Cu microstructure on the TSV-induced residual stress</a> within silicon.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Stockholm University</strong> researchers developed an <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-026-02904-0">electrically tunable superconducting diode</a> that allows supercurrent to flow in one direction while suppressing it in the other, without an applied magnetic field.</p>
<p><strong>Yale</strong> and <strong>EPFL</strong> researchers each reported advances in integrated lasers, with Yale demonstrating an <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41566-026-01984-2">Nd laser and amplifier</a> platform with a 2.9 μW threshold, 46.6 dB gain and more than 12 dBm output, and EPFL developed a <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41566-026-01985-1?">silicon-nitride laser</a> that remains self-injection locked across its full drive-current range, with sub-10-Hz linewidths and mode-hop-free 1.5-GHz chirps.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Security"><strong>Security</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Fraunhofer</strong> completed silicon validation of its <a href="https://www.iis.fraunhofer.de/en/pr/2026/press-release-risc-v-secure-element-licensable.html">RISC-V Secure Element</a> and made the OpenTitan-based design available as licensable security IP for SoCs, ASICs and chiplets. It integrates HW root-of-trust functions including secure boot, key storage and device identity.</p>
<h3><strong>Vulnerabilities and guidance</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>NIST</strong> released a draft <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/cswp/36/g/false-base-station-applying-5g-cybersecurity-and-p/ipd">5G security white paper</a> on false base stations, finding that 5G standards have reduced privacy and location-tracking risks, but devices can still be vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks.</li>
<li><strong>NSA</strong> set new <a href="https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Press-Releases-Statements/Press-Release-View/Article/4615285/nsa-announces-post-quantum-cryptography-measures-to-safeguard-national-security/">post-quantum cryptography requirements</a> for National Security Systems, including quantum-resistant support for new commercial systems beginning in 2027 and phaseout of incompatible legacy systems by 2030.</li>
<li>A major data breach at the Pentagon&#8217;s Defense Manpower Data Center <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/pentagon-breach-exposed-sensitive-data-3-million-people/story?id=136832909">exposed the unencrypted personal information of over 3 million people</a>. The breach came as a result of a security vulnerability in the agency’s file-sharing system.</li>
<li><strong>Citrix</strong> disclosed eight new vulnerabilities affecting its Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway products, <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/09/27/critical-zero-day-vulnerabilities-exploited-citrix-netscaler-adc-gateway">including two actively exploited critical, zero-day vulnerabilities</a> that can enable remote code execution, according to CISA. All of CISA’s alerts for the week can be found <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories">here</a>.</li>
<li>A security researcher uncovered an access-control vulnerability in <strong>Flock Safety&#8217;s</strong> infrastructure that <a href="https://flocksurveillance.org/formal-research-paper.html">exposed ArcGIS location data</a>, allowing him to map more than 300,000 Flock-associated surveillance devices across the U.S.</li>
<li><strong>PWC </strong>released a report finding that 84% of security and finance leaders <a href="https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/news-room/press-releases/2026/senior-leaders-cyber-budget-rise.html">expect cyber budgets to rise</a> over the next year amid rising AI threats.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Vehicles, Batteries"><strong>Vehicles, Batteries</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Architecture shift</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>The shift toward <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-defined-vehicles-push-compute-memory-and-validation-limits/">AI-defined vehicles</a> is pushing automotive compute, memory bandwidth, data movement, and validation requirements higher. Automakers are weighing centralized versus distributed architectures as increasingly data-heavy AI workloads strain in-vehicle networks, power budgets, and long-term safety verification.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Automotive chips</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Infineon</strong> launched a new family of <a href="https://www.infineon.com/technology-news/2026/inftn202609-145">digital angle sensors</a> designed for demanding motor control applications in automotive and industrial markets.</li>
<li><strong>AMD </strong>released a new <a href="https://www.amd.com/en/blogs/2026/amd-expands-automotive-grade-fpgas.html">automotive-grade FPGA built for ADAS sensor</a> applications.</li>
<li><strong>POLYN </strong>is delivering its custom engineering chip, designed to support AI-enabled braking systems <a href="https://polyn.ai/polyn-delivers-first-vibrosense-tms-engineering-sensor-nodes-for-customer-evaluation/?utm_source=site&amp;utm_medium=linkedin&amp;utm_campaign=vslaunch">through tire-road friction detection</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Microchip</strong> expanded its automotive Ethernet portfolio with new <a href="https://www.microchip.com/en-us/about/news-releases/products/microchip-expands-single-pair-ethernet-portfolio-with-new-10base-t1s-devices">10BASE-T1S transceivers and integrated endpoints</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>AVs, EVs</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>A <strong>U. of Michigan team</strong>, with <strong>Toyota</strong> funding, developed a <a href="https://news.umich.edu/steering-wheel-communicates-for-better-semi-autonomous-driving-performance/">specialized haptic steering wheel</a> designed to make semi-AV systems easier for drivers to use.</li>
<li><strong>Rivian</strong> issued a noncompliance safety recall for software that caused <a href="https://rivian.com/support/article/recall-information">rearview camera visibility</a> problems in its R1T, R1S, and R2 vehicles.</li>
<li><strong>Delta Electronics</strong> is collaborating with <strong>Nvidia</strong> on <a href="https://www.delta-americas.com/en-US/news/delta-electronics-to-advance-next-generation-autonomous-driving-built-on-nvidia-hyperion">autonomous-driving systems</a>.</li>
<li><strong>GM</strong> and <strong>LG Energy Solutions</strong> plan to produce <a href="https://news.gm.com/home.detail.html/Pages/topic/us/en/2026/sep/0929-ultium-cells-lmr-tennessee.html">lithium-manganese-rich prismatic battery cells</a> at their Tennessee plant for future GM EVs. GM says the cells are designed to deliver 33% higher energy density than LFP at comparable cost.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Quantum"><strong>Quantum</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Hardware</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Alice &amp; Bob</strong> proposed a faster approach to <a href="https://alice-bob.com/newsroom/alice-bob-new-approach-stabilising-cats/">stabilizing</a> microwave resonator cat-qubits in superconducting quantum systems for compact designs that generate less heat.</li>
<li><strong>Xanadu</strong> and <strong>Bluefors</strong> are developing a modular cryogenic system for utility-scale photonic quantum computers, aimed at <a href="https://investors.xanadu.ai/news-releases/news-release-details/xanadu-and-bluefors-partner-redefine-cryogenic-infrastructure">cooling large arrays of single-photon detectors</a> without requiring industrial-scale cryogenic plants.</li>
<li><strong>QCi</strong> introduced its Dirac-3S <a href="https://quantumcomputinginc.com/news/press-releases/2026/quantum-computing-inc.-announces-dirac-3s-advancing-speed-scale-and-solutions-for-quantum-optimization">photonic quantum system</a>, built for large optimization problems. The system has been demonstrated with up to 9,980 variables, versus 949 for the current Dirac-3.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>QC training/ infrastructure</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>New Mexico</strong> opened the <a href="https://edd.newmexico.gov/press-releases/roadrunner-quantum-lab-opens-in-albuquerque/">Roadrunner Quantum Lab</a> in Albuquerque, giving quantum startups shared access to dilution refrigerators, a multi-node quantum network, testbeds, and demonstration facilities. <strong>California</strong> announced a $30M investment in quantum and deep-space research, alongside new quantum-workforce initiatives.</li>
<li><strong>XeedQ</strong> will install a 4-qubit room-temperature quantum computer at <a href="https://www.fcps.edu/news/quantum-leap-public-education-fcps-plans-host-worlds-first-k-12-quantum-computer">Skyview High School</a> in December, which Fairfax County Public Schools says will be the first operational quantum computer in a K-12 school.</li>
</ul>

<ul>
<li>Cascaded random access <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-026-03418-w">quantum memory</a> (<strong>Stanford, SLAC, UChicago </strong>et al)</li>
<li><a href="https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1149/1945-7111/aea500">Superconducting Damascene Interconnects</a> from Electrodeposition &amp; Solid-State Metal Exchange (<strong>UAlabama</strong>)</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Workforce, Education"><strong>Workforce, Education</strong></h2>
<p><strong>SEMI</strong> says semiconductor workforce shortages are increasingly concentrated in advanced packaging and experienced manufacturing leadership. The U.S. could <a href="https://www.semi.org/en/blogs/comparing-the-semiconductor-talent-shortages-across-north-america-emea-and-southeast-asia">need 88,000 new engineers by 2029,</a> while nearly 30% of Europe’s semiconductor workforce is expected to retire by 2030.</p>
<p><strong>University of Arkansas</strong> launched the <a href="https://news.uark.edu/articles/82951/research-institute-to-drive-semiconductor-innovation">Arkansas Research Institute for Electronics Systems</a> to expand semiconductor research and train undergraduate and graduate students.</p>
<p data-pm-slice="1 1 []">A second federal judge <a href="https://immigration-analytics.com/2026/10/01/federal-court-vacates-100k-h-1b-fee-policies-in-global-nurse-force-v-trump/?">blocked enforcement of the $100K H-1B fee</a>, ruling that immigration agencies failed to follow required notice-and-comment procedures. The Sept. 30 order also prevents agencies from enforcing the fee under the administration’s September extension while the ruling remains in effect.</p>
<p><strong>ETH Zürich</strong> professor <strong>Onur Mutlu</strong> has made his 2026 <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7503492174462918657/?utm_source=share&amp;utm_medium=member_desktop&amp;rcm=ACoAAABrPN4BwKkM7TLM7PLtF9Kc0DF6C8O6srg">Digital Design &amp; Computer Architecture course freely available online</a>. The course starts with transistor and digital-logic fundamentals and progresses through Verilog, microarchitecture, pipelining, out-of-order execution, branch prediction, GPUs, memory systems, caches, and emerging computing architectures.</p>

		<title>The Hidden Challenges of Edge AI Design</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/the-hidden-challenges-of-edge-ai-design/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/the-hidden-challenges-of-edge-ai-design/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Ann Mutschler]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 07:13:48 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Top Stories]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Cadence]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge AI development]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge AI security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Efficient Computer]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Imagination]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Infineon Technologies]]></category>

		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282186</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>As models evolve faster than silicon cycles, chip architects must balance flexible compute, data movement, and defense-in-depth security.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/the-hidden-challenges-of-edge-ai-design/">The Hidden Challenges of Edge AI Design</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Successful edge AI design requires prioritizing long-term architectural adaptability, memory bandwidth, and system-level efficiency over raw peak NPU TOPS.</li>
<li>The mismatch between fast-evolving AI models and long silicon development cycles makes hardware-software co-design and heterogeneous compute increasingly important.</li>
<li>Security must be built into the hardware from the start to protect against software supply chain risks, data breaches, and silent perceptual fault injection.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>The rapid buildout of the edge is forcing chip architects and design teams to rethink how they add AI to vertical market applications. The fundamental challenge is a mismatch in timelines, because engineering teams must design for AI models, workloads, and deployment requirements that inevitably will shift long after silicon decisions are locked in.</p>
<p>Compounding this, real-world edge performance rarely depends on peak NPU TOPS. More often, it depends on memory bandwidth, latency, power budgets, security, and data movement. To keep pace with evolving models, architects are leaning heavily into flexibility — embracing heterogeneous compute, programmable data paths, expandable memory, secure field updates, and tight hardware-software co-design.</p>
<p>But flexibility alone isn&#8217;t enough. AI introduces broad attack vectors across models, data, keys, firmware, and inference pipelines, so robust security must be architected into hardware from day one. At the same time, fragmented toolchains across runtimes and frameworks make hardware-aware optimization just as important as raw compute.</p>
<p>This structural shift is redefining standard component boundaries.</p>
<p>&#8220;CPUs are becoming more GPU-like as they try to do more and more parallel processing,” observed Rob Fisher, senior director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/imagination-technologies/">Imagination Technologies</a>. “NPUs are becoming more GPU-like as they try to become more flexible, and the convergence point is with the CPU, NPU, and GPU in the middle. We&#8217;re finding more customers are trying to hedge their bets against the future than trying to squeeze out every last drop of performance today. That means we&#8217;re no longer just looking at a GPU you can slot in that just does GPU-like things. This has system-level impacts on the whole SoC.&#8221;</p>
<p>When designing edge applications with AI as a product feature, chip architects and design teams have many considerations. Hardware choices drive these broader architectural decisions, but the challenge reaches well beyond NPU TOPs.</p>
<p>“AI model performance depends on architectural details for memory, latency, power, and security,&#8221; said Eduardo Montanez, vice president and head of PSOC Edge MCUs &amp; Edge AI Solutions for <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/infineon-technologies/">Infineon&#8217;s</a> IoT, Compute &amp; Wireless Business. This is why the company’s edge microcontrollers include memory expandability, a low-latency architecture, and energy efficiency to enable battery-powered applications at the edge. They also include security features that are designed to protect data and software IP.</p>
<p>AI applications at the edge are already challenging chip architects and design teams to keep up with rapid changes in models and workloads.</p>
<p>“As new networks are continually popping up, any solution needs to be programmable to accommodate new networks and ever-changing activation functions and corresponding data types,” said George Wall, product marketing group director at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a>. “At the same time, there are hard performance requirements that must also be met.”</p>
<p>This makes hardware-software co-design increasingly important. “AI models, NPUs, memory hierarchy, and optimization techniques such as quantization, pruning, and distillation must be jointly optimized to achieve efficient deployment,” noted Niranjan Sitapure, group product manager for generative AI at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>.</p>
<p>The entire pipeline also must be optimized, because success depends on sensor ingestion, data preprocessing, inference, post-processing, and ongoing model lifecycle management.</p>
<p>Ideally, chip architects and design teams would have a detailed view of what an edge application will do, including the models it will use, required performance, available memory, and power constraints, so they can design a chip for optimal PPA.</p>
<p>“Unfortunately, that isn’t reality,” said Paul Karazuba, vice president of marketing, Silicon IP at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/rambus-inc/">Rambus</a>. “Even compressed, the chip design cycle will predate the release of any product that contains the chip by a year or more. During that time, it’s reasonable to assume the edge application will evolve, including changes to the underlying model(s) and perhaps the available memory and power. This application evolution forces chip designers to concentrate their efforts on creating chips that can adapt to changing requirements, including but not limited to a focus on moving data efficiently and securely.”</p>
<p>For others, AI acceleration isn&#8217;t the biggest challenge. What limits chip performance and efficiency may depend on the rest of the application.</p>
<p>“But architects and designers don&#8217;t design for that. They focus on neural network acceleration, claiming very high but theoretical TOPS numbers that no real application even comes close to achieving,” said Graham Gobieski, chief technology officer and co-founder of Efficient Computer. “In fact, in many real workloads (e.g., sensor fusion, autonomy), a majority of the application still runs on whatever general-purpose but very inefficient core exists on the SoC. The real opportunity to enable intelligent applications isn&#8217;t a faster NPU; it&#8217;s making the other 80% of the application as efficient as the AI portion.”</p>
<p>Beyond efficiency, edge AI applications add numerous design challenges.</p>
<p><strong>Core design challenges</strong><br />
Performance depends on more than the compute capabilities of the programmable processor being used. “For example, memory bandwidth must be sufficient to keep the computational units fed with data, and the data needs to be in a location that is easily accessible by the processor,” explained Cadence’s Wall. “Otherwise, the computational elements will basically sit underutilized. Determining workload requirements is difficult because chip designers won&#8217;t necessarily have insight into the networks consumers will be running 3 or 5 years from now.”</p>
<p>This challenge is compounded by the fact that edge AI is fundamentally a constraint-driven design problem. “You are dealing with tight power budgets, limited memory, mixed sensor inputs, and latency expectations that users feel immediately. The architecture has to be efficient before it can be intelligent,” Rambus’ Karazuba said.</p>
<p>As AI models evolve rapidly, system architectures need memory scalability for large data sets and AI models, along with enough memory for the non-AI portions of a design.</p>
<p>“Also, the design must allow for end-to-end, secure provisioning and deployment, allowing for field updates without compromising valuable data and software IP,” Infineon’s Montanez noted.</p>
<p>Moving model weights and activations between DRAM and compute engines can consume more power than the AI computation itself. “AI models evolve faster than silicon development cycles. New architectures, operators, and generative AI workloads emerge continuously, creating pressure for hardware platforms to remain adaptable,” Siemens’ Sitapure said. “For critical/high-risk applications, edge systems such as ADAS, industrial automation, and robotics require predictable latency, high reliability, and operation even with limited connectivity.”</p>
<p>While data movement can dominate performance and efficiency, other challenges may be overlooked. “The first is simple but challenging,&#8221; said Efficient Computer’s Gobieski. &#8220;The intelligence has to fit on the device. This means a lot of engineering goes into squeezing a neural network into on-device memory before any application code runs. The second has a standard answer that backfires. Splitting the application across an NPU, CPU, and DSP might seem like playing to each block&#8217;s strengths, but it complicates development by requiring many different toolchains, and it spends the savings moving data between them.”</p>
<p>Hardware teams also face non-negotiable physical constraints, especially strict low-power budgets. Thermal dissipation limits and battery constraints dictate computational efficiency, along with demanding reliability requirements for mission- and safety-critical edge deployments, Sylvain Guilley, co-founder and chief technology officer at Secure-IC, a Cadence company, noted. “Solving these core challenges requires moving beyond proprietary, siloed hardware tricks toward broader industry-wide alignment on architectural standards. To build standard open framework specifications for edge hardware, Cadence is tackling this in a new OCP FCSA Sub-Project Workstream.”</p>
<p><strong>Security from the start</strong><br />
Electronics developers looking to add AI to edge devices should incorporate several security technologies from the beginning of system design.</p>
<p>The starting point is a secure platform, followed by a secure application. “A secure platform is fundamental,&#8221; said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management for security solutions at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. &#8220;It establishes the foundation, but it does not automatically make the application — or the AI’s output — trustworthy. Developers must still address authorization, data protection, output validation, connected-service security, and component assurance at the application layer. Assume the AI platform already provides a root of trust, secure boot, attestation, encrypted communications, and trusted execution environments. That establishes the foundation, but it does not automatically make the application — or the AI’s output — trustworthy.”</p>
<p>At the application layer, Neustadter said developers must address additional controls, including:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Authorization</strong>: Ensure that only approved users and services can perform sensitive actions.</li>
<li><strong>Data</strong> <strong>protection</strong>: Handle sensitive information appropriately throughout its lifecycle.</li>
<li><strong>Output</strong> <strong>validation</strong>: Check AI results before they drive decisions or physical actions.</li>
<li><strong>API</strong> <strong>and</strong> <strong>cloud</strong> <strong>security</strong>: Protect connected services, even though edge deployments place greater emphasis on the device itself.</li>
<li><strong>Model and component assurance</strong>: Verify models, AI engines, plugins, and other third-party components before deployment.</li>
</ul>
<p>A common misconception is that an AI result must be trustworthy simply because the AI runs on a secure platform. Consider a mobile robot whose model reports that a hallway is empty. If the software accepts that result without further checks, the robot could move and collide with an unexpected obstacle. “The AI provides an input to the decision. It should not be the sole basis for the final decision,” Neustadter explained. “The application should evaluate the model’s confidence score and complete additional checks before authorizing an action. It should also apply relevant rules and safety policies and confirm the environment before the device acts.”</p>
<p>Establishing a resilient platform also does not guarantee privacy. Secure hardware does not compensate for insecure application-level data handling. For example, a smart camera in a mall may analyze shopper behavior. Even if the device is secure, storing those analytics in an unencrypted database could let an attacker access private customer information.</p>
<p>“Secure hardware does not compensate for insecure application-level data handling. Developers should encrypt sensitive data and enforce access controls throughout its lifecycle. They should also retain data only as long as necessary and limit its use to authorized people and services,” she said.</p>
<p>Models should also be authenticated with controls comparable to secure boot. Before loading a model, the system should verify its identity, integrity, signature, and provenance. This is another reason a strong root of trust is essential. “Model confidentiality and access control should also be incorporated into the system’s key-management strategy,” Neustadter explained.</p>
<p>Edge AI systems may require additional keys. A third-party model provider, for example, may want to prevent the device owner or other parties from accessing the model without authorization. Model confidentiality and access control, therefore, become part of the overall key-management strategy.</p>
<p>All models and components can introduce software supply-chain risks. Developers often rely on open-source models, AI engines, plugins, and other external components. A model that contains a hidden backdoor can generate incorrect or malicious outputs, and secure hardware may still execute it if the system accepts the model as trusted.</p>
<p>“Secure hardware will still execute a compromised model if the system accepts it as trusted. To reduce the risk, developers should therefore verify provenance and integrity, validate suppliers, use trusted repositories, and maintain software bills of materials,” Neustadter added.</p>
<p>When designing security into edge applications and mitigating attack vectors introduced by AI, engineering leadership should involve high-level product management as early as possible. That allows developers to perform risk analysis and determine where mitigations are needed across both hardware interfaces and software layers, Cadence’s Guilley said.</p>
<p>“This early architectural grounding directly informs overall device strategy in terms of cyber-resiliency,” he noted. [&#8220;Establishing this foundation early] allows us to treat cybersecurity not as a cost but as an investment that enables subsequent operations to unfold safely 24/7 and to turn incidents away from emergencies and rather have them be seen as a business continuity plan.&#8221;</p>
<p>This unified security and governance framework becomes especially important when engineering complex cyber-physical systems that must comply with cybersecurity, AI, and data privacy mandates.</p>
<p>“Design teams must continuously navigate strict regulatory boundaries, specifically around the E.U. Cyber Resilience Act, statutory requirements concerning capturing personal data in personally identifiable information, and the overarching statutory mandates enforced under the broader E.U. AI Act,” Guilley said.</p>
<p>A root of trust and separation between secure and non-secure code are also important. “Having a bootloader that manages code authentication is critical,” Infineon’s Montanez said. “With AI moving to the edge, most products still have a hybrid approach with the cloud, allowing for OTA or other communication. Therefore, edge AI applications can require additional security for the connectivity link.”</p>
<p>Big picture, security must be anchored in hardware, from secure boot and trusted firmware to protected keys, memory, and model assets. AI increases the stakes because models, inputs, and outputs can all have significant economic value.</p>
<p>“One should consider that economic value is not just the models themselves or the data inside those models, but also the financial and legal implications of a third party tampering with that data,” Karazuba noted.</p>
<p>Introducing AI into an edge device adds capabilities and features that were often unavailable in prior non-AI-enabled versions. “Device makers must design AI-enabled edge devices with a stronger security profile, given the increased financial and legal implications of a security breach,” he said.</p>
<p>Encryption is another key element, Siemens’ Sitapure said. Model weights, training data, and inference pipelines should be encrypted and protected from tampering, extraction, and unauthorized access.</p>
<p>Above all, security cannot be an afterthought. “Malicious actors could try to hack the underlying model weights and insert their own model that disrupts subsystem operation or exploits other security vulnerabilities in the system,” Cadence’s Wall said. “Fortunately, approaches range from localized encryption/decryption engines to a dedicated security island.”</p>
<p>More broadly, the most dangerous failure in edge AI is not a crash, but a live system that keeps operating while silently believing the wrong state. Real-time decisions increasingly depend on the integrity of on-device inference because edge AI is deployed in cameras, robotics, vehicles, and industrial systems that rely on NPUs, GPUs, and TPUs for performance and efficiency, but are not typically designed to ensure inference integrity under fault conditions.</p>
<p>In a recent white paper that includes the experimental block diagram and physical setup used for fault injection and measurement, Keysight security researchers showed that precisely timed fault injection (FI) can corrupt the output of a production-class edge AI pipeline without modifying firmware, model weights, software configuration, or input data. On a commercial Rockchip RK3568 platform running YOLOv5s_ReLU, most faults had no observable effect or only shifted confidence scores, but a smaller fraction induced missed detections, phantom objects, and rare high-confidence misclassifications while the system continued to operate normally. The impact can reach beyond individual inference errors. When corrupted detector outputs feed downstream tracking systems, even brief or low-probability errors can be filtered as transient noise, latched into persistent tracked objects, or amplified into denser and longer-lived false system states.</p>
<p>In the observed sequences, repeated, bounded faults transformed transient detector errors into sustained false perceptions that persisted beyond the original fault window. Once represented as system state, these errors can influence alerts, automation logic, and operator decisions while the platform appears healthy, which has implications for product teams. Here, traditional measures of resilience, such as uptime or fault recovery, may be insufficient for AI-driven systems. Resilience also must include inference integrity and the ability to prevent corrupted outputs from becoming trusted system state.</p>
<p>At the same time, decentralizing compute offers a foundational safety advantage in some applications, reducing how much sensitive information can leave the device. “Running inference on the device means sensitive data never travels, so there is no communication channel to intercept, and decentralized processing means there is no central repository of sensitive data to breach,” Efficient Computer’s Gobieski said. “A compromise costs you one device, not the fleet. The model itself carries the usual concerns about what it exposes, but those are far smaller than the ones you eliminate by keeping the data on the device.”</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion</strong><br />
Navigating the edge AI landscape requires a mindset shift for engineering teams. Success no longer hinges just on maximizing theoretical peak compute, but on balancing silicon longevity with rapid software evolution. By prioritizing flexible architectures, hardware-software co-design, and defense-in-depth security from day one, chip designers can build resilient platforms that adapt to whatever AI workloads emerge — even after the chip architecture is finalized.</p>
<hr />

As the semiconductor ecosystem pivots to AI, it is transforming how IP is created, verified, managed, and sold.</p>
