		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282171</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>The shift from software-defined to AI-defined vehicles raises questions about whether the hardware can keep up. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-defined-vehicles-push-compute-memory-and-validation-limits/">AI-Defined Vehicles Push Compute, Memory, And Validation Limits</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Automakers are making different bets on compute architecture, with some favoring large central processors while others distribute specialized compute across AI-defined vehicle systems.</li>
<li>Moving sensor data is becoming as important as processing it, with raw camera and radar data putting new demands on memory, interfaces, in-vehicle networks, and power efficiency.</li>
<li>AI-defined vehicle systems must verify sensor inputs, AI decisions, and updates across edge cases and over a vehicle’s long service life.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>Carmakers are racing to develop and incorporate advanced AI capabilities into vehicles in order to capitalize on what is expected to be a $1 trillion-plus market for physical AI over the next decade.</p>
<p>To be competitive in this market, automakers will need to upgrade today&#8217;s software-defined vehicle systems to automotive electronics frameworks that can efficiently handle the memory, compute, and power demands in these systems.</p>
<p>“A software-defined vehicle is one whose functionality evolves through software updates after it leaves the factory, but an AI-defined vehicle goes a step further, using AI to continuously interpret data, make decisions, and adapt behavior in real time,” said Paul Karazuba, vice president of product marketing for Silicon IP at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/rambus-inc/">Rambus</a>. “The difference is not just software that changes, but intelligence that actively shapes how the vehicle operates.”</p>
<p>But effectively leveraging that intelligence requires rethinking the automobile&#8217;s basic architecture, the supply chain for parts and data, and the methodology for creating, integrating, testing, and monitoring adaptable complex systems of systems under harsh ambient conditions.</p>
<p>“AI is not a value proposition in itself, but an essential enabling technology for the continued evolution of SDVs and AI-defined vehicles,” said Moritz Neukirchner, senior director of cross-portfolio growth and strategic alliances, Elektrobit<b>.</b> “AI has been part of vehicles for many years — in perception stacks for advanced driver assistance systems, for example. What changes with the AIDV is the experience. Functionality becomes visible and directly accessible to customers, while AI accelerators and development capabilities become more accessible to software developers. The first customer-facing applications naturally center on speech assistants and conversational interfaces. At the same time, the evolving developer experience is enabling less visible but equally important applications, including AI-assisted remote diagnostics and observability solutions that help monitor, understand, and maintain vehicle software throughout its lifecycle.”</p>
<p>Enabling this transition will provide semiconductor companies with several enhanced revenue streams. “The transition to the so-called ‘AI-defined’ vehicles can be seen as the next generation of software-defined vehicles,” said Paula Jones, senior director of automotive at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/infineon-technologies/">Infineon</a>. “Currently, traditional OEMs are working toward SDVs, where software defines key features, built on hardware building blocks of zone control modules, central compute, and standard communication along with AI features and over-the-air updates. This is a good opportunity for semiconductor companies like Infineon to provide the critical hardware and software elements, including automotive-qualified microcontrollers, Ethernet, and sensors to drive this upcoming generation of SDVs, defined by AI.”</p>
<p>Exactly how system designers will enable those advancements is not yet defined, and different OEMs are approaching the same problems differently.</p>
<p><b>Betting on compute architecture</b><br />
One of the biggest questions facing the developing ecosystem hinges on how centralized a vehicle’s compute architecture should be. OEMs usually choose one of two approaches to compute architecture — a more centralized, compute-power-first solution with larger chips, or more distributed “right-sized” architecture.</p>
<p>“Different OEMs are making different bets,” said Michal Siwinski, executive vice president, chief product and marketing officer, and general manager for security solutions at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/arterisip/">Arteris</a>. “It will be interesting to see what ends up happening a few years down the line. You want to make sure these things are in production deployment for years, not for months. We will know in a few years whether both approaches are equal. Right now, it’s too early to tell. There is a bit of a tug-of-war going on.”</p>
<p>Both approaches have their pros and cons. “The ‘server-on-wheels&#8217; is basically going for max compute. It&#8217;s all about throughput, performance, and maximizing your power envelope,” said Siwinski<b>.</b> “The more compute you have, the better the mindset. It’s a bit of a brute force approach, but you can have that. You build these amazing super chips. You put a bunch of them in the car, and they can be the central compute for everything. Let’s say you&#8217;re building something you want to be very safe and very secure. At the same time, it is a single point of failure. If you take more of a distributed architecture, it&#8217;s different. You can have a more best-in-class solution, and you&#8217;re not doing one-size-fits-all compute because you can optimize. This chip says it&#8217;s going to be doing this for that application, and you have more of a pick-your-best. So it&#8217;s kind of the classical situation where you ask if it is better to have built one thing that does everything or have something that&#8217;s more purpose-built?”</p>
<p>The AI-defined vehicle push has designers experimenting with a variety of chip architecture solutions. “One of the additional problems is people are using GPUs for more and more things that they haven&#8217;t used GPUs for in the past,” said Rob Fisher, director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/imagination-technologies/">Imagination Technologies</a>. “Whereas they might have used an NPU to do AI processing previously, they may now look at the GPU as an excellent way to do AI processing. This isn&#8217;t typically done today, so we have a whole new realm of possibilities that we need to consider.”</p>
<p>Chiplets also offer some intriguing possibilities for AI-defined vehicles. “We have a vision at Cadence that chiplets will be a new way of delivering technology, and one of the reasons is that you can make chips application-specific, and we are now making systems that are getting much more complex, with AI at the edge everywhere,” said Sylvain Guilley, chief technology officer at Secure-IC, a <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a> company. “This means, in any robot or car, you will have the same need for compute, the same need for AI inference and even safety functions, at different locations. It&#8217;s much more economical to use the same chiplets across the full system. Chiplets are going to play an important role because we are redefining autonomous systems that have many different sensors.”</p>
<p><b>Data and memory bottlenecks</b><br />
When designing these AI-defined vehicle systems, figuring out the most efficient way to move sensor and communications data is as important as figuring out what to process it with.</p>
<p>“AI workloads are generating more data than ever, and feeding processors efficiently is becoming just as important as the compute itself,” said Rambus’ Karazuba. “The biggest bottlenecks are data movement, power efficiency, and system trust. Feeding processors efficiently is becoming just as important as the compute itself. At the same time, automotive systems must deliver that performance while meeting strict safety, security, and reliability requirements over a vehicle&#8217;s lifetime.&#8221;</p>
<p>With AI sensors constantly pulling in new data, the key challenge is finding more powerful solutions that work at a practical cost. “The <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_cloud">point cloud</a> is a lot more data to move to a central processing unit that is much more powerful than what we see in classic and traditional ECUs. How do we get the data there?” said Sven Kopacz, autonomous vehicle section manager at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/">Keysight Technologies</a>. “Just think of a rear camera. You put the vehicle in reverse, you want the picture on your screen, so you need to tell the camera that you&#8217;re on now. So that&#8217;s what, 20 bytes? It&#8217;s a small message you want to send in that direction. But now you have the camera stream coming in this direction. This is an asymmetric connection, and we cover it with what we call SerDes, which is optimized for asymmetric use cases. In a car, if you can save 10 cents on a module, you will go for that. Same for the wiring. We also see the automotive OEMs moving to optical now, because if you go with Ethernet and you want to wire up every peer with another one, you end up with a lot of extra wiring.”</p>
<p>These new workload demands are also pushing automotive OEMs to rethink who they trust to support their data processing. “We have a lot more data to process in the car, and also to transport,” said Kopacz. “Now OEMs are moving toward a point where they say, ‘We want to differentiate on how we process that data. We just don&#8217;t want to rely on a black box, so we want that point cloud. I don&#8217;t want you to do the processing. A Tier One might sell this processing module to an OEM. It could come out of the same source, but the OEM wants the flexibility to choose how they want to combine that, and they may put much more trust into a new player in the ecosystem, let&#8217;s say Nvidia, that is familiar with how to process a point cloud and do object recognition.”</p>
<p>AI-defined vehicle systems also must verify sensor inputs, AI decisions, and updates across edge cases and over a vehicle’s long service life.</p>
<p>“If you&#8217;re driving a car around for 20 years maybe, the technology that launches Day One has to stay out there, and these AIs aren&#8217;t used to that,” said Carrie Browen, autonomous vehicle business line manager at Keysight Technologies. “The AI that you and I use regularly is constantly learning and changing, but in the car it must do it right. That&#8217;s a different kind of learning: to come back, validate that decision, and validate that the loop is correct. That&#8217;s the other end of it. The data must go all the way through. It must come from the collection into the car, and then you must prove and ensure the safety of the people that are relying on those decisions are being made because of that data.”</p>
<p>The reality of these data and verification requirements also underscores the growing memory bottleneck in AV development. &#8220;What tends to matter is our ability to move the bytes, store the bytes in order to enable efficient operation,&#8221; said Rahul Rithe, director of autonomy sensing systems at Rivian, at this month’s JEDEC Automotive Electronics Forum. &#8220;To get the incremental improvement in performance, it requires an exponential increase in the compute and also in the memory, and this is really the key bottleneck that we are now running into. The memory bandwidth and capacity are the gating resources for advanced autonomy and physical AI.”</p>
<p><b>Automotive component lifecycles in the AI-defined vehicle era</b><br />
With automotive chips expected to last much longer than their counterparts in other sectors, like data centers, OEMs already are making vehicle AI architecture decisions based on maximizing lifespan. “An example of a decision that industry is making is this shift to potentially Automotive Ethernet and Optical Automotive Ethernet in the inner vehicle connectivity,” said Browen. “That way they can get rid of some of the nodes that are another physical thing that has a certain number of relays, or a certain number of switches that are associated with it. So by switching to Ethernet on that backplane, but also switching to Ethernet for those edge devices — for the devices like your seat control and your power windows, or all the little ECUs that are in the car, if that can all be on one IP, one network — you can get rid of these extra nodes. It&#8217;s a decision the industry is making to remove some of those physical components in the car for longevity reasons.”</p>
<p>Keeping AI-powered vehicles on the road longer gives OEMs an extra incentive to sell software upgrades. “OEMs are talking about even longer lifespans for the platform, because for SDVs, a future revenue stream would be selling upgrades through plain software upgrades enabling features,” Kopacz said. “They want to keep the platform alive a little longer.”</p>
<p><b>Conclusion</b><br />
The shift to AI-defined vehicles will be measured less by how much AI an automaker can put in a car than by how reliably the entire system works over its lifespan.</p>
<p>As software and models evolve after production, automakers also will need to preserve the evidence that each update behaves safely across vehicle variants and years of use. The architecture that succeeds will be the one OEMs can best deploy, validate, maintain, and afford at scale.</p>
<p>That long-term support begins during development, but it also needs to be extensible. AI-assisted engineering could accelerate delivery, but its outputs must remain traceable and reproducible.</p>
<p>“AI is driving a step change in how automotive software is designed, implemented, tested, integrated and qualified,” said Elektrobit&#8217;s Neukirchner. “This has the potential to shorten development cycles, improve engineering productivity, and make the complexity of SDV development more manageable. This depends on the resulting software and evidence remaining traceable, reproducible, and governed throughout the lifecycle. It is equally important not to repeat a common mistake in SDV programs — treating the ease of greenfield development as a reason to rebuild everything. The greater challenge is reusing existing assets to ensure commercial viability while enabling controlled evolution across vehicle platforms, variants, model years,  and generations. This continuity is essential to make AIDV development economically sustainable at scale.”</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>On-device AI can deliver faster insights, greater autonomy, and less cloud traffic — but only with the right infrastructure.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/turning-edge-ai-data-into-real-time-action/">Turning Edge AI Data Into Real-Time Action</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Edge AI is expanding across consumer, industrial, automotive, and medical devices by moving real-time intelligence closer to where data is generated.</li>
<li>Edge analytics systems deliver value only when edge devices have the right deployment, monitoring, lifecycle management, and software infrastructure.</li>
<li>Security, power efficiency, connectivity, and memory choices must be designed in from the start as edge AI systems take on more autonomous decision-making roles.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>More AI is moving out of centralized data centers and into devices that can interpret data and act on it in real time.</p>
<p>By handling more processing locally, these edge systems can sharply reduce latency, improve security and privacy, and address growing concerns about data center energy and water consumption. Some data is already processed locally in consumer, industrial, automotive, and medical applications, but that percentage is expected to grow significantly in the next few years as edge devices become more capable and smaller language models are introduced.</p>
<p>&#8220;Number one are your personal devices,&#8221; said Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>. &#8220;Those are small. For example, a watch that can track your ECG and so forth. If your heartbeat rhythm is off, you can set it up so that it calls your hospital directly. On the industrial side, for example, a control unit monitors pressure in a boiler, or a control unit monitors a particular assembly line in a given section of an automotive factory. At the very extreme edges, every time a robot is picking up something and doing something, the finger is an edge device.&#8221;</p>
<p>Vehicles contain multiple sensors and processors that process data locally. &#8220;I would say cars in general are not edge devices,&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;Edge devices are more like the lidar in the car. Lidar finds out all your obstacles and everything, then it needs to be processed on board the car. Every section of the car is an edge device, whether it&#8217;s radar, lidar, the camera, or what is sensing in the camera, which needs to make sense of what the camera is seeing. That whole system is an edge device.&#8221;</p>
<p>The medical space is also filled with intelligent edge devices. &#8220;For example, a robotic surgeon has arms and knows the position to make the cut, with the right pressure,&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;Then all the systems need to be monitored and connected so that if the patient&#8217;s heart rate goes up, or they are trying to wake up, the human needs to figure out what to do.&#8221;</p>
<p>Whatever the application, edge AI analytics focus on real-time performance and metrics that address how data is gathered, stored, and used, as well as what actions are taken based on that data. That information is then looped back to improve the process. In effect, edge AI analytics systems act as a bridge between different systems, and between people and hardware.</p>
<p>&#8220;By placing compute near data sources, edge AI infrastructure enables local inference across telecom nodes, industrial gateways, enterprise servers, and smart building controllers,&#8221; said William Chen, product marketing group director for design IP at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/cadence-design-systems/">Cadence</a>. &#8220;These systems operate at the point of physical interaction, powering applications from automotive and industrial SoCs to wearables, smart cameras, and consumer endpoints.&#8221;</p>
<p>That connection between local intelligence and physical systems depends on a steady flow of usable data, collected close to the source, and filtered before it moves farther upstream.</p>
<p>Data comes from numerous devices and sensors. &#8220;From a data‑gathering perspective, edge systems primarily ingest information from two sources — sensors and human or agent interactions,&#8221; Chen explained. &#8220;Sensors span a wide range of modalities, including vision via cameras, light, environmental, industrial, and more. They generate data at very high volumes and speeds. Examples include multi‑camera video streams captured over millisecond‑scale intervals — or faster. To make this data tractable, raw sensor outputs must be processed locally to reduce bandwidth and latency requirements before being forwarded upstream, either to a local compute cluster or directly to a cloud‑based AI factory for higher‑level processing and reasoning.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Setting up an edge AI analytics system</strong><br />
Several key considerations come into play when deploying an integrated edge AI analytics system.</p>
<p>&#8220;Organizations building edge AI systems will gain a durable advantage by tightly integrating compute, data movement, interfaces, and security models early,&#8221; Chen noted. &#8220;Once collected, all data must be transported efficiently for downstream or upstream processing steps such as reasoning, inference, and storage. These data paths span multiple hops and domains — from sensors to edge processors, between edge processors and adjunct accelerators or local memory, from edge devices to gateways, and ultimately from gateways to cloud infrastructure.&#8221;</p>
<p>Layers of software oversee all these elements, from digital twins to product lifecycle management.</p>
<p>&#8220;The key challenge is, how do you build a model for what the edge AI needs to do?&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;The second thing is, how do you connect the entire digital thread with what we see in the digital twin of the product to the digital twin in the factory? Then, how do you monitor everything, and how do you do the analytics? Finally, how do you act on it?&#8221;</p>
<p>Balasubramanian described three components to this flow:</p>
<ul>
<li>An open digital business platform that lets companies of any size work together to solve industrial challenges;</li>
<li>A product lifecycle management (PLM) software platform that helps organizations manage all data, processes, and documentation for a product from its initial design through manufacturing, service, and disposal; and</li>
<li>Edge devices deployed throughout the facility gathering data. These can include fixed sensor devices, robots, cobots, autonomous mobile robots, or an industrial arm in a production line.</li>
</ul>
<p>Silicon lifecycle management (SLM) can provide additional device-level monitoring, while PLM serves as the data backbone of an edge analytics system.</p>
<p>&#8220;You can essentially trace back everything,&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;When I ordered this part, what maintenance was done on the part on this robot? When was the last firmware update done? Who came and accessed the data? Was anything different in this particular robot compared to everything else in the factory flow?&#8221;</p>
<p>Edge AI devices can use local processing to make decisions, or some combination of local, near-local, and cloud. But the ability to act locally is only useful if the surrounding infrastructure is configured to control where data moves, how models are deployed, and when humans remain part of the decision loop.</p>
<p>Systems administrators need to deploy edge devices effectively to benefit from analytics. &#8220;Companies want to have more edge-based analytics for the purpose of keeping their data on their own localized systems, so they would set up the infrastructure to enable that to happen,&#8221; said Matthew Bubis, director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/imagination-technologies/">Imagination Technologies</a>. &#8220;There would be a human in the loop to set that up, but once it&#8217;s set up, a company or an enterprise might have an automated system of managing that. For example, if you open your company laptop and you&#8217;re using an AI-based system, the IT department would have set up a way to manage really sensitive, secure data. They would put a wrapper on that to say, &#8216;We must process this on the edge and deploy to the edge systems only so that we&#8217;re keeping all our data closed.&#8217; The data is automated, but that&#8217;s after a human has decided how the edge devices operate.&#8221;</p>
<p>The overall goal of edge AI analytics is to improve the organization&#8217;s operations. &#8220;AI is increasingly moving from the digital world into the physical world, where it can improve how systems operate, make decisions, and use resources more efficiently,&#8221; said Stephan Zizala, division president of edge systems at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/infineon-technologies/">Infineon Technologies</a>. &#8220;The next wave of innovation will not be defined by how much data we collect, but by how effectively we can turn that data into action. Across industries, organizations are looking for ways to improve operations through faster insights, greater efficiency, and more autonomous decision-making. Edge AI enables that shift by processing data close to where it is generated, whether from sensors in industrial equipment, smart homes, or robots. This allows systems to react in real time, reduces dependence on constant cloud connectivity, and helps keep sensitive information under local control.&#8221;</p>
<p>How those systems are connected depends on the operating environment, the sensitivity of the data, and the balance each organization wants to strike between autonomy, control, and cloud-based scale.</p>
<p>On one end, semiconductor fabs may keep their analytics systems air-gapped, so no data gets in or out. On the other end, a soda bottling facility may run entirely in the cloud for efficiency. Often, it&#8217;s a combination of both. &#8220;You will have a local model doing more of the regular work, but it is not working constantly all the time,&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;This is similar to how humans sleep and think through the day and get the brain to realign all the memories and skills. At some point, you will phone in to the cloud and update the models. Or if they come up with some corner cases, you need to be able to update the learning of the main model. For example, Tesla updates the software of the car.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Edge analytics security considerations</strong><br />
Protecting proprietary IP is important, along with privacy, because applications such as wearables handle personal data.</p>
<p>&#8220;In parallel to sensor data, data generated through human or agent interaction includes inputs from AI assistants, via local inference models, as well as corrections, feedback, or direct inputs from end users,&#8221; said Cadence&#8217;s Chen. &#8220;These workflows drive a strong need for privacy‑controlled edge environments, where sensitive information is retained in secure local storage and only &#8216;must‑have&#8217; and conditioned data, which has been filtered, encrypted, and policy‑controlled, is transmitted to the cloud.&#8221;</p>
<p>Security must be considered at every layer, or organizations risk impacting human worker safety in addition to financial loss through downtime or fraud.</p>
<p>The analytics layer needs specific attention. &#8220;For example, with the software that processes data and detects anomalies, triggers, and prioritizes alerts, the risks are related to decision integrity,&#8221; said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. &#8220;Analytics systems risk missing the real problems, failing to detect abnormalities, such as in a medical setting where signs of patient health deterioration are missed. It could also be fraud or equipment failures. In any of these settings, too many alerts can be created, similar to false positives, where there are repeated incorrect patient alerts. Other risks include the corruption of the analytics model itself, including hidden backdoors that allow specific untrusted users to be trusted.&#8221;</p>
<p>Edge analytics fleet management platforms and alert systems also face compromise. &#8220;For example, by allowing malicious updates, model deployment, or manipulation of a whole fleet of devices,&#8221; said Neustadter. &#8220;These types of platforms have a large — maybe one of the largest — attack surfaces, and are becoming high-value targets because edge AI deployments rely on them for device onboarding, AI model deployments and management, alerts, analytics, and policy management. There are also software supply-chain attacks, such as compromising models or updates of infrastructure even before deployment.&#8221;</p>
<p>Edge AI devices also bring specific security risks. &#8220;The biggest shift in edge AI security is that cyber attackers are moving from trying to steal information to trying to manipulate decisions,&#8221; Neustadter observed. &#8220;Edge devices are evolving to autonomous decision-makers, where a successful attack can influence not just the data collection, but real-world actions.&#8221;</p>
<p>Verifiable trust is needed across the entire lifecycle, from device authenticity and software integrity to data provenance, model integrity, and secure management, Neustadter explained. &#8220;AI model compromise includes adversarial attacks, poisoning, extraction, and unauthorized modifications.&#8221;</p>
<p>A recent NIST <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ai/100/2/e2025/final">publication</a> identified adversarial machine learning as a major emerging security concern. &#8220;For example, attackers intentionally manipulate inputs to cause AI systems to make incorrect decisions while appearing normal to humans,&#8221; said Neustadter. [1] &#8220;Model theft is another example because AI models themselves are valuable assets as companies invest significantly to differentiate in the market and secure business.</p>
<p>AI reliability/safety must also be considered, especially for medical devices, industrial automation, robotics, and autonomous devices. &#8220;An incorrect AI recommendation can create safety or operational consequences even if there is no malicious intent,&#8221; she noted. &#8220;Unlike traditional software, AI systems can make incorrect decisions even if no attacks have occurred.&#8221;</p>
<p>Those security and reliability requirements ultimately flow back into silicon choices, because edge processors must support local intelligence while meeting tight constraints on power, latency, connectivity, and trust.</p>
<p><strong>Edge AI processing chips</strong><br />
A programmable logic controller (PLC), which generally consists of a microprocessor (MPU) with a CPU, memory, and interface ICs, acts as a bridge between the sensors and AI. The AI could be processed by a low-power MCU, NPU (neural), or VPU (vision).</p>
<p>&#8220;There will be an MCU, but also the PLC running industrial edge,&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;A virtual PLC is already security-proven, so you could have that in the edge as part of your system to run and monitor everything based on what you&#8217;re getting from the PLM (product lifecycle management) thread and what you&#8217;re getting from real-time data.&#8221;</p>
<p>GPUs also have a role to play. &#8220;Traditionally, AI was always these huge, giant, data center-level cards going everywhere,&#8221; said Imagination&#8217;s Bubis. &#8220;But now we are implementing AI processing technology within our very smallest chips, because we see small chip edge AI customers who might have a tiny device in a television or a refrigerator for the home.&#8221;</p>
<p>While matrix multiplication tasks are important, edge AI GPUs are also needed for traditional graphics processing tasks. For example, a robot may have a display screen so a maintenance worker can see what&#8217;s going on. &#8220;We see the dual use case in edge AI,&#8221; said Bubis. &#8220;In automotive, that&#8217;s 100% the case, because you&#8217;ve got these ever-larger screens and displays demanding very complex graphics outputs whilst also demanding some AI workloads, either for ADAS or for the local LLMs that might be happening in the vehicle.&#8221;</p>
<p>In enterprise and client applications, various devices and widgets process data locally, with small language models and AI bots saving IT personnel time by fielding basic questions. &#8220;Extendable platforms can be connected to single-board computers to provide the ability to run heavy compute,&#8221; said Bubis.</p>
<p>Those processing choices also shape the surrounding data fabric, because edge AI systems must move information among sensors, accelerators, memory, and networks quickly enough to support real-time analytics.</p>
<p><strong>Networking and memory for edge analytics</strong><br />
Compute, interfaces, and memory all play a key role in edge analytics.</p>
<p>&#8220;How to move data reliably and efficiently has become just as important as increasing compute capability in edge AI system design,&#8221; said Cadence&#8217;s Chen. &#8220;Long adopted in the mobile system, MIPI CSI-2 serves as a preferred vision ingress interface in embedded systems, along with other USB-based and proprietary links, efficiently feeding image data into the ISP pipeline and aligning well with edge device requirements. Beyond vision, many interface protocols foundational to modern cloud AI factory architectures, such as PCIe, Ethernet, LPDDR/DDR/GDDR, and UCIe, are increasingly deployed at the edge because of their proven topologies and mature ecosystems. Given the constraints typical of edge platforms, however, designs are strongly biased toward cost‑ and power‑efficient implementations.&#8221;</p>
<p>UCIe and PCIe are both utilized. &#8220;Although UCIe is commonly viewed as a premium interconnect for high‑end AI and chiplet-centric designs, heterogeneous execution at the edge is emerging and potentially relevant for future edge designs,&#8221; said Chen. &#8220;The modularity, flexibility, and reuse enabled by chiplet architectures are increasingly compelling for edge applications that demand tailored and heterogeneous I/O mixes. PCIe 3/4/5 plays a central role in attaching high‑throughput peripherals such as accelerators, NVMe storage, and NICs, while the long‑established Ethernet standards remain widely deployed and form the backbone of most edge networking environments, ranging from 1G to 10G for devices to 25G–100G for infrastructure.&#8221;</p>
<p>Memory can also be heterogeneous. &#8220;In memory subsystems, a practical mix of DDR5, GDDR6/7, and LPDDR5X/6 has been increasingly adopted in higher-performance edge systems, optimizing capacity, bandwidth, and energy efficiency across diverse edge use cases,&#8221; said Chen.</p>
<p>While HBM and DDR may be the right choice for high-performance systems, LPDDR is a common choice for edge and embedded AI, where energy efficiency and cost are important, <a href="https://www.rambus.com/blogs/enabling-memory-choice-for-modern-ai-systems-tenstorrent-and-rambus-deliver-flexible-power-efficient-solutions/">according to</a> Rambus. Applications include computer vision, robotics, industrial automation, medical devices, and battery-powered or thermally constrained systems. The memory controller must be optimized for low-power operation, work across challenging conditions, and integrate flexibly into diverse SoC architectures.</p>
<p>Also, an edge-optimized network architecture should deliver packet-level visibility, active monitoring, and application intelligence to ensure tools never miss a thing, <a href="https://www.keysight.com/us/en/learn/hubs/network-visibility/edge-computing.html">according to</a> Keysight.</p>
<p><strong><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282176" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Keysight-edge-monitoring.png?resize=635%2C314&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="635" height="314" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Keysight-edge-monitoring.png?w=635&amp;ssl=1 635w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Keysight-edge-monitoring.png?resize=300%2C148&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Keysight-edge-monitoring.png?resize=600%2C297&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 635px) 100vw, 635px" /> </strong><br />
<strong>Fig. 1: An edge-optimized network. </strong><a href="https://www.keysight.com/us/en/learn/hubs/network-visibility/edge-computing.html"><strong>Source</strong></a><strong>: Keysight</strong></p>
<p><strong>Conclusion</strong><br />
Edge AI is a fast-growing space, particularly in the industrial sector, with new devices and use cases emerging all the time.</p>
<p>&#8220;The excitement I have is coming up with different designs and edge devices,&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;We are seeing a lot of momentum in putting intelligent devices at the edge — not just sensors, but real devices. That&#8217;s an entire system that can operate on its own, either air-gapped or connected to the internet, Wi-Fi, or the cloud. That&#8217;s the beauty of it. Essentially, you have everything connected to something, and it already has its own brain to operate.&#8221;</p>
<p>Edge AI systems need to take corrective action very quickly. &#8220;If it takes a lot of time to process and correct the mistake, then you might have a lot of defective parts already done in a car manufacturing factory, or in a GPU manufacturing fab, and everywhere else,&#8221; said Balasubramanian. &#8220;The goal is to have fewer humans involved in the factory, but to have more domain specialists monitoring it much more smartly, so that there is no downtime and the quality is always 100%. That&#8217;s the kind of metric that industrial teams look at.&#8221;</p>
<p>An end-to-end deployment flow is key. &#8220;As AI continues its journey into the physical world, sensors, intelligence, connectivity, and security must work together seamlessly,&#8221; said Infineon&#8217;s Zizala. &#8220;The real opportunity lies in creating systems that not only collect data but can understand their environment and act on it intelligently, reliably, and securely.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>Reference</strong></p>

</ol>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Distributed NVM supports high-endurance telemetry logging, functional safety, and time-sensitive networking where resilience is critical.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/memory-at-the-edge-non-volatile-memory-challenges-and-requirements-for-humanoid-robots/">Memory At The Edge: Non-Volatile Memory Challenges And Requirements For Humanoid Robots</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Humanoid robots are rapidly transitioning from research demonstrations to commercial deployment in factories, warehouses, and service environments. As adoption scales, high-performant, reliable operation increasingly depends on the underlying electronic and memory architecture. Analyst reports from Goldman Sachs suggest annual humanoid robot shipments could reach more than 6 million units by 2035, up from fewer than 15,000 units in 2025. Similar to autonomous vehicles, these systems rely on high-density sensor arrays, power-efficient semiconductors, and AI-driven processing.</p>
<h2>Zonal network framework</h2>
<p>The operational demands of a humanoid robot require a distributed, multi-tier electronic architecture.</p>
<p>A centralized compute core performs vision processing, AI model execution, and real-time motion planning. A time-sensitive network then distributes commands to MCUs embedded in limbs, joint actuators, and battery management systems (BMS).</p>
<p>A humanoid robot platform typically employs multiple memory technologies – each selected to address and optimize design challenges related to performance, power consumption and reliability. AI inference and perception workloads require high-bandwidth memories to support large neural networks, while distributed motor control sub-systems powered by dedicated MCUs prioritize deterministic low-latency operation <sup>[1]</sup> and power-loss persistence to maintain control state at the edge. Different subsystems therefore place fundamentally different demands on memory, ranging from bandwidth-optimized storage for AI workloads to latency-optimized memory for real-time control functions. Within this broad spectrum, reliability-related characteristics become particularly important for distributed edge controllers to achieve real-time control.</p>
<p>Humanoid robots must continuously monitor actuator health, joint loads, and system stability to prevent failures that could affect safety, reliability, or availability. To support fault diagnostics, root-cause analysis, predictive maintenance, and regulatory traceability, these systems capture large volumes of operational telemetry. Logging motor torque, velocity, and limb position data at sampling rates above 10 kHz can quickly exceed the endurance limits of conventional non-volatile memories. As a result, reliable operation depends on selecting memory technologies optimized for the requirements of each subsystem.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282128" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig1.jpg?resize=735%2C363&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="735" height="363" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig1.jpg?w=735&amp;ssl=1 735w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig1.jpg?resize=300%2C148&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig1.jpg?resize=600%2C296&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 735px) 100vw, 735px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Zonal processing and networking architecture in humanoid platforms.</strong></p>
<p>High-bandwidth DRAM supports AI inference and perception workloads, while NAND Flash stores operating systems, AI models, and application software. These centralized memories are optimized for bandwidth and storage density. In contrast, distributed non-volatile memories support boot management, networking infrastructure, telemetry logging, and functional safety, where endurance, deterministic latency, and power-loss resilience are often more critical than capacity. This article focuses on the unique requirements of that distributed memory layer.</p>
<p>This network layout shown in Figure 1 isolates computing workloads by subsystem. As a result, each domain has distinct memory requirements. In evolving humanoid architecture, high-capacity processing is centralized at the core, while high-frequency control loops are managed locally by individual zonal MCUs and edge motor controllers, as shown in Figure 1.</p>
<h2>Technical bottlenecks in edge sensing and actuation</h2>
<h3>Page-write latency and state fracturing</h3>
<p>Standard Flash and EEPROM devices introduce a 5 to 10 ms page-write delay. During this process, data is staged in a volatile buffer while internal charge pumps program the memory cells. If a humanoid experiences a power failure or sudden emergency-stop during this window, the active position log fractures. Upon reboot, the joint controllers lose absolute coordinates, forcing a potentially disruptive and time-consuming mechanical homing sequence to re-calibrate.</p>
<h3>Thermal acceleration and data retention decay</h3>
<p>Mechanical friction and electrical power dissipation within compact joint housings drive internal temperatures above +100°C. Elevated thermal stress degrades the oxide insulation layer in legacy charge-based NVMs, causing trapped electrical charges to leak from the cells, shortening data retention lifespans. In contrast, crystal-polarization memories store data through atomic alignment rather than trapped charge, eliminating this leakage mechanism.</p>
<h3>EMI-induced bit flips</h3>
<p>High-torque BLDC motors generate significant EMI and stray magnetic fields near joint-control electronics. This noise can induce bit errors and voltage disturbances that corrupt telemetry data and affect system stability.</p>
<h2>Subsystem memory matrix and requirements</h2>
<p>While there is no universally accepted humanoid memory architecture, most platforms combine centralized computing resources with distributed control and networking infrastructure.  Table 1 illustrates representative volatile and non-volatile memory requirements across these three commonly found functional domains in a humanoid platform.</p>
<table style="border-collapse: collapse;" border="1">

<td style="padding: 5px;"><strong>Memory type</strong></td>

<p><strong>Table 1: Memory technology requirements by subsystem.</strong></p>
<p>Memory selection ultimately depends on application-specific requirements including latency, endurance, density, functional safety, power consumption, and cost targets.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282132" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig2.webp?resize=939%2C435&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="939" height="435" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig2.webp?w=939&amp;ssl=1 939w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig2.webp?resize=300%2C139&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig2.webp?resize=768%2C356&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig2.webp?resize=600%2C278&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 939px) 100vw, 939px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Memory requirements across key humanoid robot functions.</strong></p>
<p>To address these localized hardware constraints (see Figure 2), persistent memory requirements can be examined across the three representative functional domains in Table 1: F-RAM for joint-level data logging, functional-safety compliant NOR Flash for the compute platform, and standard NOR Flash for networking infrastructure.</p>
<h2>How specialized memories fit the architecture</h2>
<p>To see how these requirements translate into physical silicon deployments, we look at the total memory distribution per robot frame. Figure 3 illustrates the allocation metrics and joint attachment counts required to sustain stable telemetry and boot functions.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282133" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig3.webp?resize=984%2C481&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="984" height="481" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig3.webp?w=984&amp;ssl=1 984w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig3.webp?resize=300%2C147&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig3.webp?resize=768%2C375&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig3.webp?resize=600%2C293&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 984px) 100vw, 984px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: Typical memory distribution within a humanoid robot.</strong></p>
<p>This physical distribution highlights the widespread use of distributed non-volatile memory throughout the humanoid platform, spanning edge-control subsystems (joint control, motor drives, and battery management), networking infrastructure (TSN switches and zone controllers), and centralized compute functions (AI processing, HMI, and system boot).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282134" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig4.webp?resize=939%2C477&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="939" height="477" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig4.webp?w=939&amp;ssl=1 939w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig4.webp?resize=300%2C152&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig4.webp?resize=768%2C390&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-fig4.webp?resize=600%2C305&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 939px) 100vw, 939px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 4: Representative memory placement within humanoid control modules.</strong></p>
<h3>Motor control &amp; BMS layer: Eliminating wear-out via F-RAM</h3>
<p>Motor control boards and battery management systems (BMS) rely on continuous data-logging for real-time edge processing. As shown in the module layouts in Figure 4, a standard platform deploys a dense network of serial F-RAM components to manage this streaming telemetry.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282135" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-table2.webp?resize=1344%2C674&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1344" height="674" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-table2.webp?w=1344&amp;ssl=1 1344w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-table2.webp?resize=300%2C150&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-table2.webp?resize=1024%2C514&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-table2.webp?resize=768%2C385&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infineon_NVM-for-humanoid-robots-table2.webp?resize=600%2C301&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Table 2: Edge memory requirements and corresponding memory characteristics.</strong></p>
<p>F-RAM offers write endurance of more than 100 trillion cycles, enabling continuous high-frequency logging without practical wear-out concerns. Under high-frequency logging workloads, memory endurance can become a key design consideration when selecting non-volatile storage technologies.</p>
<p>F-RAM data state transitions occur via atomic polarization alignment in less than 100 nanoseconds. This enables random access at bus speed with immediate non-volatility. Position data remains preserved during power loss, allowing operation to resume without a full re-homing sequence.</p>
<h3>Main compute &amp; HMI: Functional safety NOR Flash</h3>
<p>SPI NOR Flash and high-performance serial Flash devices, including Octal SPI memories, provide the read throughput needed for responsive HMI interaction. Functional safety NOR Flash devices can support ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 requirements through features such as hardware ECC and protected boot mechanisms. Beyond functional safety, modern humanoid robots also require cybersecurity safeguards. Secure boot mechanisms help verify firmware authenticity during startup, while cryptographic validation techniques protect firmware integrity throughout the system lifecycle. Authenticated update capabilities further reduce the risk of unauthorized software modifications, helping maintain reliable operation in connected industrial and commercial environments.</p>
<p>To connect these core systems to the limbs, dedicated SPI Flash components pair directly with TSN Ethernet switches, streaming network firmware via high-speed SPI/QSPI interfaces with minimal timing jitter to prevent communication lag down the chassis.</p>
<h3>Connectivity backbone: Time-sensitive networking nerves</h3>
<p>The central compute core communicates with the individual limbs via a high-bandwidth Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) Ethernet protocol backbone. To maintain deterministic packet routing across the chassis, dedicated high-speed SPI NOR Flash components pair directly with the system&#8217;s industrial Ethernet switches. These memories stream network configuration firmware via multi-I/O SPI interfaces with minimal timing jitter. This helps maintain deterministic communication between the central controller and individual joints, supporting synchronized motion across all axes.</p>
<p>While DRAM and NAND Flash provide the bandwidth and storage capacity required for AI workloads and operating systems, distributed control architectures introduce a separate class of memory requirements. Edge controllers, motor drives, and battery management systems prioritize deterministic latency, endurance, and power-loss resilience, making specialized non-volatile memory technologies an important complement to the central memory subsystem.</p>
<h2>Conclusion</h2>
<p>Humanoid robot architectures place diverse demands on non-volatile memory subsystems, ranging from high-endurance telemetry logging at the edge to functionally safe firmware storage in centralized compute platforms. Matching memory technologies to the specific requirements of each subsystem can improve system reliability, availability, and deterministic operation as humanoid deployments scale.</p>

		<title>Open Security Foundations Are Only The Beginning: Deploying Caliptra Hardware in Production</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/open-security-foundations-are-only-the-beginning-deploying-caliptra-hardware-in-production/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/open-security-foundations-are-only-the-beginning-deploying-caliptra-hardware-in-production/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Vincent van der Leest]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 07:07:44 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Security Matters]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Caliptra]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[open hardware]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[open source]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Rambus]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Roots of trust are beginning to assume a broader role as platform security orchestrators.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/open-security-foundations-are-only-the-beginning-deploying-caliptra-hardware-in-production/">Open Security Foundations Are Only The Beginning: Deploying Caliptra Hardware in Production</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>As AI models, training data, and proprietary workloads become more valuable, the need to protect them rises concurrently. Data center security has always been mission critical, but the imperative for more robust and effective safeguards is higher than ever. This is occurring in an environment of growing complexity where data center architectures are becoming increasingly heterogeneous, with CPUs, accelerators, SmartNICs, DPUs, memory subsystems, and specialized controllers working together to execute ever more demanding workloads. This architectural evolution delivers impressive performance gains, but it also creates a significant challenge: trust must be established across a large and complex collection of devices.</p>
<p>With attackers increasingly motivated to target the lower layers of the system stack, security can no longer begin at the operating system. It must start in hardware, with a trusted foundation that establishes device identity, verifies the integrity of code, protects cryptographic assets, and enables trusted attestation throughout a device&#8217;s lifecycle. In other words, it must start with a Root of Trust in hardware.</p>
<p>This growing need for a common trust framework is one of the reasons the industry is exploring Caliptra technology, an open-source silicon Root of Trust architecture designed for data center-class devices.</p>
<h2>Why the industry is considering Caliptra</h2>
<p>Hardware Roots of Trust have traditionally been tailored to the security, performance, and lifecycle requirements of individual products. These purpose-built implementations remain essential for many applications, but differences in architecture, interfaces, and trust models can make it more complex for cloud providers and infrastructure operators to establish consistent trust across hardware from multiple suppliers.</p>
<p>Caliptra provides an open-source silicon Root of Trust architecture for data center-class devices. It defines common mechanisms for device identity, measured boot, and attestation that can help improve consistency across implementations. With support from several cloud and semiconductor companies, the project is emerging as one approach to greater alignment on hardware trust.</p>
<p>Its open development model allows security architects to review the architecture, firmware, documentation, and implementation details. This transparency supports evaluation, collaboration, and interoperability across the ecosystem. For organizations considering Caliptra, it provides a shared technical framework that can complement the differentiated security capabilities required for production deployments.</p>
<p>End-customer requirements are also driving increased adoption. Cloud and data center operators increasingly expect chip suppliers to provide Caliptra trademark-compliant implementations, giving customers greater confidence that Caliptra has been integrated in accordance with the project&#8217;s defined requirements. To qualify, vendors must complete a conformance process in which their architecture and implementation are evaluated against the Caliptra integration checklist.</p>
<p>Caliptra&#8217;s growing momentum raises an important question. Once the decision to adopt Caliptra has been made, what comes next?</p>
<h2>Selecting Caliptra is not the same as deploying Caliptra</h2>
<p>For many engineering teams, selecting a Root of Trust architecture appears to be the difficult decision. In practice, however, the real work often begins after that choice has been made. An open-source Root of Trust establishes a valuable foundation, but commercial deployment introduces requirements that extend well beyond the baseline implementation. Development teams must determine how trust will be extended across the wider SoC, how cryptographic services will be exposed to software, how secure boot will be coordinated across multiple subsystems, and how attestation will integrate with platform management frameworks.</p>
<p>Additional challenges quickly emerge. Certification objectives must be defined. Secure provisioning flows must be implemented. Lifecycle management policies must be established. Software interfaces, drivers, and applications must be developed and maintained. Organizations also need a strategy for long-term maintenance, support, and vulnerability remediation.</p>
<p>These requirements are not unique to Caliptra. They are realities associated with operationalizing any hardware security architecture. However, they often become visible only after teams move beyond the evaluation phase and begin preparing a product for deployment. As a result, the industry conversation is increasingly shifting from Root of Trust adoption toward Root of Trust deployment.</p>
<h2>The Root of Trust is evolving into a security orchestrator</h2>
<p>There is another important trend that is reshaping hardware security architectures. Traditionally, a Root of Trust functioned primarily as an isolated security anchor. It protected keys, verified software integrity, and established an initial chain of trust. While these capabilities remain essential, today&#8217;s complex platforms often require something more comprehensive.</p>
<p>Modern data center devices contain multiple processors, memories, accelerators, firmware domains, and management subsystems, often supporting workloads from multiple tenants on shared infrastructure. Security policies must therefore span the entire platform, protecting tenant data, workloads, and cryptographic assets across these interconnected components rather than within a single security block. As a result, Roots of Trust are beginning to assume a broader role as platform security orchestrators.</p>
<p>This orchestration function can include coordinating secure boot across multiple domains, managing lifecycle states, supporting system-level attestation, enforcing security policies, and maintaining trust relationships across the entire SoC. Rather than acting solely as an isolated security module, the Root of Trust becomes the coordinator of platform-wide trust.</p>
<p>As systems continue to become more heterogeneous, this broader visibility and control may prove just as important as the traditional security functions themselves.</p>
<h2>What production readiness really means</h2>
<p>Moving from a reference implementation to a deployable security architecture requires more than adding features. Production readiness typically includes secure execution environments, protected key storage, lifecycle management frameworks, integration software, certification preparedness, and robust software interfaces. It must also account for cryptographic change, providing the agility to adopt new classical, post-quantum, or regional algorithms as standards and requirements evolve. Development teams additionally require documentation, maintenance processes, and a clear model for long-term ownership and support.</p>
<p>Side-channel resistance and fault injection protections become increasingly important as products move into real-world deployment environments. Certification-oriented development often requires clearly defined security boundaries and supporting documentation. Even seemingly straightforward tasks such as software integration can consume significant engineering resources when they must be developed entirely from scratch.</p>
<p>Viewed collectively, these requirements illustrate why deployment often becomes the most demanding phase of the security journey.</p>
<h2>Bridging the gap between foundation and deployment</h2>
<p>This deployment challenge is the motivation behind Rambus CryptoManager Root of Trust for Use with the Caliptra Specification. Rather than modifying or replacing Caliptra, it operates alongside an unchanged Caliptra implementation. This allows chip vendors to retain the implementation needed to pursue Caliptra trademark compliance, while the CryptoManager Root of Trust extends trust across the broader SoC and adds the infrastructure required for commercial deployment.</p>
<p><em> <img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282225" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Rambus_Open-Security-Deploying-Caliptra-fig1.webp?resize=1070%2C581&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1070" height="581" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Rambus_Open-Security-Deploying-Caliptra-fig1.webp?w=1070&amp;ssl=1 1070w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Rambus_Open-Security-Deploying-Caliptra-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C163&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Rambus_Open-Security-Deploying-Caliptra-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C556&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Rambus_Open-Security-Deploying-Caliptra-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C417&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Rambus_Open-Security-Deploying-Caliptra-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C326&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></em></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: CryptoManager Root of Trust and Caliptra integration.</strong></p>
<p>CryptoManager provides a secure execution environment, protected key and data storage, platform-level security orchestration, dedicated Caliptra drivers, system applications, and an integration framework intended to simplify deployment. It also supports a broad range of classical, post-quantum, and regional cryptographic algorithms through a programmable architecture designed to accommodate crypto agility for future evolution.</p>
<p>At the platform level, the CryptoManager Root of Trust helps coordinate secure boot, attestation, lifecycle management, and security policy enforcement across the wider SoC. Advanced side-channel and fault-injection countermeasures provide additional protection for security-sensitive operations, while certification-oriented design principles help support development efforts targeting frameworks such as FIPS 140-3, PSA Certified, and SESIP.</p>
<p>The objective is straightforward: allow engineering teams to spend less time constructing security infrastructure and more time focusing on product differentiation.</p>
<h2>Conclusion</h2>
<p>Open security foundations are becoming an increasingly important part of the semiconductor industry. Caliptra is helping establish a common framework for trust across data center and AI infrastructure, providing a foundation that many organizations are now choosing to build upon.</p>
<p>But adopting a common foundation is only the first step. Engineering teams must still transform that foundation into a secure, supportable, and production-ready deployment capable of protecting increasingly valuable workloads and data. CryptoManager Root of Trust for use with Caliptra specification is designed to help bridge this gap by operating alongside an unchanged Caliptra implementation and adding platform security orchestration, certification readiness, cryptographic agility, lifecycle management, and the integration infrastructure required for commercial deployment.</p>
<p>The question facing the industry is no longer whether a common Root of Trust framework is needed. The question is how to operationalize that trust across increasingly complex systems. By combining Caliptra&#8217;s common foundation with the production-ready capabilities of CryptoManager, organizations can accelerate their path toward secure AI and cloud infrastructure.</p>
